articles.title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?
articles.summary: BBC Verify has looked at how much Burnham's new spending commitments cost and how they will be paid for
articles.body:
Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.

He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.

BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about £1.5bn.

Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line.

In his speech outside Downing Street on Monday, Burnham said his "first instruction" would be "to end rough sleeping in our country".

The most recent official data suggests that there were around 4,800 people sleeping rough on a single night in England in 2025, up from 1,800 in 2010.

The government announced that Burnham's "instruction" would be delivered by £340m of spending, which it said would support at least 3,000 people over a five year period.

It said this money would come from existing "uncommitted" budgets in the housing department.

This means that the funding has been made available by the Treasury to the department but had not yet been assigned to a specific project.

On Tuesday morning the Treasury announced that it would cut VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, knocking an estimated £45 from the typical household's annual bill from the autumn.

It said this would cost £850m in 2026-27 - to be funded by scrapping the previous government's digital ID scheme, which had been estimated to cost £1.8bn over the next three years.

However, the Office for Budget Responsibility, the official spending watchdog, made clear in the last budget that the digital ID scheme was itself "unfunded" at that stage.

That implies that while scrapping the digital ID scheme will reduce a spending pressure on the government it will not, in itself, pay for the VAT cut.

That tax cut will have to be funded in the next budget, either by tax rises or specific spending cuts elsewhere.

Five headaches Andy Burnham will have to deal with as PM

Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high

Can Andy Burnham solve the housing crisis?

On Wednesday, the government announced it would reduce the cap on bus fares in England from £3 to £2 from 1 January 2027, though this does not include London.

It estimated this cap would cost the Department for Transport more than £500m.

It said most of this would be found by replacing grants for international climate projects with loans. This would save the government money because the loans would be expected to be paid back in full, plus interest, freeing up funds to pay for the bus cap policy.

But there are still uncertainties with this approach, said Max Warner from the Institute for Fiscal Studies.

"It's not clear how much we would expect to be paid back nor what the interest rates will be," he said.

On Thursday the government announced it would cut business rates for pubs , clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from April 2027, saving a typical pub £1,100.

It estimated that this tax cut would cost the Treasury around £100m a year.

The government claimed it would be "fully funded" but did not provide details, beyond stating that part of the cost would be met by "reviewing reliefs for businesses that do not make a positive contribution to local communities, such as vape shops". It did not state what other kinds of businesses would fall into this category.

The Starmer government had already announced a business rates support package for pubs in England in January, with a 15% cut applying in the current financial year of 2026-27 and a real-terms freeze in their rates for the subsequent two years.

At that time officials estimated that package would cost £80m in its first year, and the cost in the subsequent two years would be calculated in due course by the Office for Budget Responsibility.

The latest business support for pubs from the Burnham government will come on top of that earlier support - so the Treasury will have to provide an official costing for the overall package announced since January in the Autumn budget.

Cost: Downing Street says no additional cost to taxpayers, funded

Burnham ended his first week as PM by working out of the new No 10 North , based at Heron House in Manchester's city centre, which he claimed will be the "situation room for making Britain better".

He's expected to work from there each week, with other ministers including Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster Louise Haigh, who is overseeing the department as part of her role, also working there on a regular basis.

Up to 300 civil servants are expected to join the operation by the end of the next year, but Downing Streets insists it will cost taxpayers no extra money.

"The running of No 10 North will be covered by existing Cabinet Office budgets. There is no additional cost to taxpayers", Burnham's spokesman told reporters earlier this week.

These pledges add up to about £1.5bn. That might sound like a lot, but they are small commitments relative to overall government spending, which is projected to be around £1.4 trillion (£1,400bn) this year - making it about 0.1% of total public spending.

The bigger question is whether Burnham is likely to follow through with some of the more expensive policies he's previously signalled, including reforming social care or expanding council house building.

Burnham earlier this week indicated he could raise the income tax personal allowance , which the Institute for Fiscal Studies has estimated could end up costing £8.5-9bn but the idea of this happening imminently was downplayed within days.

Chancellor John Healey is likely to want to take defence spending from 2.7% to 3% of GDP by 2030, given he resigned as Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the Treasury's failure to commit the money to do that. But that would cost an additional £9bn a year in today's money.

Burnham has also promised the "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period". While the details are unclear, estimates from the Centre for Cities think tanks suggest that to match the English council house building rates of the 1950s to the 1970s would require another £13bn a year in public subsidy.

Policies on this scale, which could run into several billions, would likely need to be set out in future budgets and spending reviews, alongside detailed plans about how they would be paid for.

However, Burnham has said he will stick to the government's existing fiscal rules - not borrowing for day-to-day spending and having debt fall as a share of the economy by the end of the Parliament.

That means any major new spending commitments would likely require difficult choices: such as raising taxes or cutting spending elsewhere.

articles.title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
articles.summary: While the US tariffs imposed on the UK are effectively unchanged, other countries now have a better deal.
articles.body:
It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.

From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.

Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.

Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.

These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.

In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.

The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.

What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.

While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.

The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.

At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).

It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.

The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.

The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.

This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.

US hits dozens of countries with new wave of tariffs

What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?

There should be scope for a better deal for the UK, but it raises an interesting question about whether the government will pursue an EU-style ban. This is widely seen as a backdoor way to target China, in particular for conditions in its Xinjiang province.

Last October the government said it "remained firmly opposed to the use of state-imposed forced labour", but that it was "considering how best to reflect this position," citing "operational and legal complexities".

Since then, the UK has welcomed imports of Chinese cars, and is exploring a services trade deal with the country. The relationship with China has been a balancing act for the government.

This is also one of the global stories of the tariff wars. As the US repeatedly changes its rationale for tariffs, the rest of the world is focused on trading with each other. For example, Canada increased its trade with the rest of the world by more than it lost from the US.

China's total dollar trade with the US is flat in the first half of this year versus last year. Across the world it is up 21%, including 14% with the EU, 11% with the UK, and 24% with Africa.

There could be pressure now to legislate for a formal ban on forced labour products. Successive governments have opted for a lighter voluntary due diligence regime.

Will the US force a change in the UK and elsewhere, and what might it offer in return?

Or the UK may opt to keep its precarious geopolitical position by sticking to its existing deals in medicines, metals and cars.

articles.title: Behind the scenes at No 10 as Andy Burnham becomes prime minister
articles.summary: Laura Kuenssberg was given unprecedented access to the new prime minister’s first days in power.
articles.body:
"You can clap now," a Downing Street official with a clipboard instructed the staff eagerly lining the halls of No 10 in the moments before the new prime minister walked in.

The applause duly began before the famous door opened, so the first sight and sound to greet Andy Burnham and his wife were crowds of clapping staff, crammed into the Downing Street hall. They stretched up the long corridor all the way to the door of the Cabinet Room - left ajar for him to walk straight in and get down to work.

I've seen plenty of prime ministers come and go from outside No 10. But I'd never been allowed inside at that moment before , able to hover outside the Cabinet Room and grab a quick word with the country's new leader at such an intense, symbolic time.

I have rarely seen a politician look as thoroughly delighted as Burnham, pride bursting out of his buttoned-up suit - that's right, the T-shirt and bomber jacket didn't make it to No 10 - or a leader who has wanted to stop and shake as many hands.

No 10 staff are already wondering if they'll ever be able to stick to a regular prime minister's schedule, normally designed with military precision. If Andy Burnham was able to take the time to stop and speak to everyone in the country, I suspect he probably would.

It's a sign of his different style that our team was given permission to be behind the scenes at three key moments in the 59th prime minister's first week in charge - when he became Labour leader, when he walked into No 10, and on day one at his new Manchester outpost, No 10 North.

Most important by far was our half-hour interview in that shiny new office, after weeks during which Burnham was chased by accusations he'd avoided tough questions. But the extra glimpses we were given, alongside Burnham's own voracious appetite for social media, display a prime minister that's not just at ease in front of the cameras, but a leader who wants to bring you along for the ride.

They included revealing moments that are normally hidden - his first steps into the Cabinet Room to appoint his team, rating pub snacks with his Chancellor, John Healey, in an Instagram post , and sharing pictures with us of the family dog, Axel, whom he describes as having "angry little man energy".

"Comms" - how politicians communicate and explain themselves and talk to the public - is not the be-all and end-all.

Burnham's exploits online have already brought mockery and launched a thousand memes. But if a leader can't get your attention to make their arguments - as Keir Starmer found so challenging - ultimately, they are not going to get very far at all.

And the biggest difference of the Labour reboot so far is how the government looks and sounds. They've put an obvious priority on punter-friendly announcements such as cutting VAT from energy bills and tax breaks for pubs - although it is important to note the details on how to pay for all of that are not yet clear.

For Burnham though, telling his story is the easy part. Joking about the unique stink that accompanies Scampi Fries, or showing me his gold disc on loan from The Smiths' guitarist Johnny Marr, won't help him deal with US President Donald Trump, find money for defence, or create a new service to care for the elderly and vulnerable in England. Nor will it be any use as he grapples with the country's huge debts, changing demographics or public concerns about immigration.

Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.

Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.

But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.

Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".

When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024 .

But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?

And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.

What about welfare? Remember Sir Keir ditched most significant reforms in the face of resistance on the back benches. While seeking not to "blame" anyone receiving benefits, Burnham said the country had to "get serious" about getting the welfare bill down, and suggested he might make it harder for some people to claim, by imposing extra conditions.

He didn't want to give much away about where he was going to find extra billions for defence, or pay for public services. He repeated that he'd stick to the promises on income tax, VAT and National Insurance made in 2024. But the prime minister clearly pointed to a possible shake-up of the council tax system, where those with the most expensive properties might have to pay considerably more. Changes like that to council tax, or to welfare, would be huge political moves that would put him on a collision course with some of his party, and some political opponents too.

Then, when it comes to matters of war and peace, which for Burnham are genuinely new, it felt we could see him thinking in real time how to answer the question, perhaps trying to balance giving a flavour of who he is, without creating a political accident.

Does he trust Trump? Twice he wouldn't say.

"It's a changing world," his second answer.

Would he take a call from Russian President, Vladimir Putin?

A pause, then: "I'd have to know the circumstances".

As mayor, Burnham evidently spent years thinking hard about how to use power, and how he wants to shift the balance in the UK away from Westminster. The impact of that stance could be profound, way beyond some admirably shiny No 10 signs emblazoned all over one floor of a government building in Manchester.

Mayors are expected to get power to spend nationally collected income tax, and crucially to spend billions without strings.

Burnham spent time too as mayor absorbing people's experiences, their hardships and frustrations.

"My strength always is in remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change because I am prime minister," Burnham told me.

Although don't be in any doubt, he also spent time thinking and planning about how to make a return to the political heart of this country, the Westminster he believes is so flawed.

But when it comes to the gravest matters that prime ministers have to deal with - security, power around the world, or the country's long-term economic stability, we're perhaps yet to see if Burnham's ambition for No 10 is accompanied by truly new big ideas that match the scale of his rhetoric.

There are worries on the right of the Labour Party that Burnham has not absorbed the reality of the country's economic position - years of stuttering growth, and sky-high levels of debt that leave the UK incredibly vulnerable to the financial markets' judgements, whether he likes it or not.

And concerns on the left, that he's tickled their bellies with promises of "authentic Labour", flirting with the ideas of increasing state control of vital industries, but which might not come through. And like most incoming prime ministers, he has precious little experience of handling international events. The moments in our interview where he was least sure-footed were answering questions about how he'd manage relationships with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.

One minister said he'd "vibe left, but govern from the centre". Perhaps, as he's tried to give firms and families a "breathing space" when it comes to the cost of living, he'll ask for "breathing space" from the public before his complete programme becomes clear.

Burnham has long been unusual as a politician - a leader who has managed to be popular in a time when politicians often disappoint and are sometimes despised. He knows he's walking into a job that's been marked by failure for a decade. As he told me, "the onus is on me not to be another one who just doesn't change things". He's part of a political generation he proclaims to be "just not good enough".

Remember, his own career has had plenty of failure too. It took Burnham three goes to become the leader of his party. As he arrived, straightening his tie, to be confirmed in the top job in central London 10 days ago, I asked him why he'd taken so long.

He laughed and told me, "I like to make an entrance".

Andy Burnham has now truly arrived. But he knows all too well, there won't be applause everywhere he goes.

articles.title: Are the 'luteal uglies' a real thing?
articles.summary: More women than ever are talking about the luteal phase on social media, but how does it actually affect you?
articles.body:
"Is it just me or am I the ugliest person alive?" a woman in her early 30s asks the camera on TikTok, accompanied by the caption "POV: Girls in their luteal phase."

The video has 2.4 million views and hundreds of comments.

"This is literally me," one woman writes. "I'm angry at how accurate this is," another says.

There are thousands of videos like this one on social media, lamenting the "luteal uglies" - the changes in appearance and mood that women say appear during the luteal phase of their menstrual cycle.

During this phase, which occurs in the second half of a woman's cycle and ends when she gets her period, women experience a huge drop in oestrogen. So are the "luteal uglies" a real thing?

According to Dr Louise Newson, a GP and women's hormones specialist, this change in hormone levels means women can experience a shift in their appearance, sleep and mood during this time.

"Our hormones affect our skin, they affect our collagen, so a lot of people find their skin becomes drier, their complexion not so bright, they might have acne and spots," Newson explains. "They might get bloating and breasts can change shape."

'I feel like my brain is working in slow motion'

Elena Spaven, 25, can relate to the TikTok videos and says she feels "extremely bloated" during the second half of her cycle.

"My skin feels dull and textured and just looks more tired in general, and my chest feels heavier and sore."

That's because when your oestrogen falls in the days before your period, progesterone rises, ramping up oil production in your skin, explains Dr Helen O'Neill, an associate professor in reproductive and molecular genetics at University College London.

During this hormonal shift, your body holds on to more fluids, meaning you may end up with a puffier face, general bloating and tender, swollen breasts.

Elena, who works in hospitality and as an actress in London, says she feels lethargic and "completely unmotivated" during her luteal phase.

"I feel like my brain is working in slow motion, I tend to become clumsy and way more forgetful," she says. "I don't want to socialise as much and I feel low."

Newson says that while women are starting to talk more about the impact of their cycles, many still do not know what to do about it.

"These women are genuinely suffering and it's affecting their ability to work, function, socialise and just exist," she says.

The response to women's concerns can also be frustrating, she adds.

"Would you say to a man 'Oh your testosterone is down, just don't go to the gym, have a duvet day?' It's unacceptable that women have to put up with it."

Your relationships may also change during the luteal phase, Newson says - which is something freelance journalist Henrietta experiences.

"If I find myself wanting to get irritated with my wonderful, hilarious, chilled out partner there's an extremely high chance I haven't had my coffee, haven't eaten or that I am in my luteal phase," said the 30-year-old.

It also affects her friendships. "With my friends, I tend to either overshare and regret it, or isolate myself from them and regret it."

Henrietta can experience a sense of "despair and distress" during her luteal phase, including feeling as though she is useless or having "intense flashbacks to embarrassing or upsetting experiences".

Her symptoms, which include blurry vision, struggling to recall "basic words" in conversation and feeling unfocused, can be embarrassing to deal with at work, she says.

She wishes there was more awareness of the issue. "There are still widespread misconceptions surrounding how and why hormones impact women's health and wellbeing."

When her period arrives, she feels relief.

Newson says that the luteal phase is not something women can just "snap out of", and that women can often be wrongly made to feel that their symptoms are normal, or that they are overly emotional.

People can dismiss these symptoms as "just PMS", says 36-year-old business owner and mum-of-two Charlotte Dodds, whose symptoms include bloating, spots on her face and a lack of concentration.

These can be a "big knock" to her confidence, particularly when working with clients - she runs a business community called Baking Bosses which helps people build baking businesses from home.

"But when you're self-employed, like I am, your calendar can't just stop because your hormones are changing."

More education and discussion about menstrual cycles are needed, says Elena, who only learned about the luteal phase through social media at the age of 24.

O'Neill says there is "so little education that women receive about the fundamental aspects of how their bodies work".

So much so that many women have turned to TikTok for help.

In one video, which has 2.4 million views, a young woman asks: "Ladies, what do you do during your luteal phase to feel better?! I honestly can't cope any more."

There are thousands of comments, with one follower suggesting to "wear baggy clothes and avoid the mirror", and another saying "eat chocolate".

Another writes that the luteal phase makes her "avoid my husband", while someone else says they cope by watching television "with a bottle of wine".

But this advice may actually be detrimental - so what can help women cope with their luteal phase symptoms?

Understanding that it's a "predictable, temporary phase" is important, says O'Neill

Nutrition is key during the luteal phase, she adds - and staying hydrated can help reduce puffiness

Easing off salty foods, reducing alcohol intake, and keeping up movement can all help too

Steering clear of processed foods and alcohol will help you avoid increased inflammation, Newson explains

You should see a health professional if you are particularly struggling during the luteal phase, Newson adds, encouraging women to advocate for themselves

"If people don't get what they think is acceptable in the first, second, third, appointment they should go and see someone else. These symptoms don't usually go on their own," she says.

articles.title: The real reason child vaccination rates are falling
articles.summary: As child immunisation rates fall across the UK, one clinic in west Yorkshire is taking aggressive steps to boost immunisations
articles.body:
Twenty-week-old Grayson easily could have become one of the tens of thousands of British babies left unvaccinated against polio.

His mother, Lily, agrees with the principle of immunisation. But overwhelmed by the early weeks of motherhood, and suffering from post-partum depression after a traumatic birth, she was daunted by the prospect of a long journey to a doctor's surgery. "I've been through the trenches, awake all night. You don't want to leave the house, or go to a different town."

Weeks ticked by, and eventually Grayson missed the polio and diphtheria jabs he was supposed to get at eight weeks old. By that point he was officially classed by the NHS as "overdue" for vaccination; effectively, he was on his GP's naughty list.

Then Lily realised there was a clinic practically on her doorstep - at a location she hadn't expected.

That clinic - in Keighley, West Yorkshire - runs from a vacant retail unit at the Airedale shopping centre, a 1960s-era precinct that locals say has fallen on hard times in recent years, with plenty of empty, boarded-up units. The staff who created the clinic thought: why not use one of those vacant units to administer vaccines?

"This was an empty shop; there was nothing here, the windows were all blacked out," Flora Jennings, a local charity coordinator, tells me over the sound of a baby's laughter, on the morning I visit the clinic.

It's an imaginative solution to a national problem. Over the last 15 years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across Britain. The share of five-year-olds in England who have received a four-in-one jab (which protects against viruses like polio and tetanus) is now 81%, down from 89% in 2014. About 84% have received both of their recommended MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) jabs, down from 88% a decade ago.

"If you just look at the generalised population, the decline doesn't look horrific," says Prof Dan Hungerford, an epidemiologist at the University of Liverpool who gave evidence to Parliament on this topic. "But if you compare us to other nations, particularly our European neighbours, we are one of the worst-performing countries in terms of getting early-life vaccinations to children."

Politicians are now asking how Britain - the country of Edward Jenner, the "father of immunology" - could have allowed its immunisation rates to drop so low, and what could fix it.

One Labour MP on the Health Committee has gone further, telling the BBC that it's time to consider a policy that's commonplace in some countries, but still something of a taboo in Britain: mandatory childhood immunisations.

Before the 1800s, between 40% and 50% of children in Europe died before their 15th birthday. Now, in Britain that number is well below 1%, according to the UN.

Scientists broadly agree that vaccines were key to this improvement.

"Along with clean water and sanitation, immunisations have had a profound impact on keeping children alive," says Ben Kasstan-Dabush, a lecturer in global health policy at the University of Edinburgh.

And that's why some find it so worrying that Britain's rates have slipped. Last year alone saw measles outbreaks in parts of Birmingham, Bristol, and north London; so far this year, two children in England have died of the disease.

In January, MPs on the Health Committee described the backslide as "national disgrace".

Some blame the rise of misinformation on social media. Last year, a group of American scientists found that reading just one anti-vax Facebook comment about the HPV jab - given to teenagers - was enough to make some parents hesitate.

But all of the public health experts who spoke to the BBC said that whilst anti-vax social media sentiment plays its part, they don't think it's the main reason immunisation rates have slipped.

Instead, they point to something more mundane: they think that parents of young children simply have fewer face-to-face contacts with medical professionals than they did 10 or 15 years ago.

Beccy Baird, a senior fellow at the King's Fund think tank, says that despite colourful media reporting around "anti-vaxxers", most parents who turn down vaccination are not ideologically opposed to it. Convenience plays a big role, she says; vaccination rates are highest when parents regularly interact with medics, who can remind them to get their children jabbed and tell them exactly where to do it.

And those interactions have become rarer. England has seen a 45% decline over the last decade in the number of health visitors (nurses and midwives who treat young children at their home), according to BBC analysis. It's part of a health visitor's job to remind parents about vaccines and, in some cases, administer jabs directly.

And over roughly the same period, the number of fully trained GPs in England struggled to keep up with rising patient demand, according to British Medical Association data; while the Nuffield Trust think tank suggests that patients have become less likely to see the same GP on repeated visits - meaning families don't build trusted relationships with doctors they recognise.

"Those touch points have become fewer," says Kasstan-Dabush.

At Keighley's shopping centre, inside the vaccination clinic, nurses are passing around biscuits.

"The kitchen's there, the playpen's there," says Jennings as she points to a soft-play where parents can leave children while their siblings are vaccinated. "I wanted it to be really inviting, almost like you're walking into someone's home."

The idea of opening a vaccination clinic inside a town centre shopping arcade seemed odd to some of the staff when it was first suggested.

Now, they say it's key to the clinic's success. "We need to make it simple, we need to put services where people come," says Jennings. It means they can catch casual shoppers who "pop their head around the door" and decide on a whim to get their child vaccinated.

"We're right in the centre. And down here it's flat, so you don't have to push a pram up a hill." She says some parents simply won't attend a clinic if it involves more than one bus.

And in the families come. Over the morning, the clinic vaccinates 10 infants, some of whom are classed by the NHS as "overdue". In many cases, the parents actually turn up to use a different service, like baby weighing, but once they are inside, lead GP Dr Zoyah Hussain gently suggests an immunisation - and most parents say yes.

"I do get a lot of questions… 'why do we need to give them jabs?', 'why don't we just let nature manage itself?'," Hussain says.

There's Lily, the 18-year-old who finally gets her son Grayson his polio and diphtheria jabs. And there's Keeley, an assistant in a ceramics shop, who arrives with her baby Luca, and is impressed by the clinic's convenience, with no need for an 08:00 phone call or complicated online form. "It's easy-peasy," she says.

Most of the young mothers have come across online anti-vax posts. "I see these things on Facebook where it's like, don't give your child vaccines because it's got ADHD in them," says Lily. Indeed, Hussain says she still hears parents asking if the MMR jab causes autism, a full 28 years after a link was suggested in a now-discredited paper by the former doctor Andrew Wakefield.

The clinic - which serves a relatively poor community - has vaccinated hundreds of infants since 2023, helping to boost coverage in an area that's historically had a low rate of immunisations. As of March this year, 88% of the children registered with Modality AWC (the GP practice that runs the clinic) now receive their first MMR dose by the age of 18 months, up from 78% three years ago.

"We are bucking that national trend," says Bill Graham, a senior administrator at the practice.

So what can be done about falling vaccination rates across the rest of the country?

One option is to emulate the Keighley model, and open walk-in clinics in vacant retail units. Jennings argues there are crumbling shopping centres all over the country, hit by online shopping, that could do the job.

Baird, from the King's Fund, agrees that vaccination works best when it's carried out in small, easy-to-access local venues - like shopping centres - rather than large, intimidating vaccine hubs that might involve a long journey. In a paper, she studied the roll-out of Covid vaccines in Gloucestershire - and found that "vaccines delivered locally through… familiar community venues - instead of mass-vaccination centres - made access easier, more trusted".

She says: "If you put it in Tesco car park, people will get it."

But some experts are sceptical. Whilst schemes like Keighley's can help on the margins, they say, at the national level a much bigger answer is needed. Hungerford says that child poverty is a key driver of vaccine refusal; parents who have to worry about bills often don't have the brain space to think about immunisations, he says.

And some are pushing for more radical solutions.

Labour MP Paulette Hamilton, a former nurse who was recently interim chair of Parliament's Health Committee, tells the BBC it's time for a "national conversation" on whether child vaccinations should be "opt out" rather than "opt in" (though she stresses she is not speaking on behalf of the committee).

"We were a country that was free of some of these childhood illnesses, and now it's just getting really bad," she says. "The conversation should be about, do you get a small payment [for getting your child vaccinated]? Do you make it mandatory, so you opt out rather than opt in? Is it that we need more education?."

She didn't specify what an "opt out" policy would look like, but various US states already do it. In Texas, a child needs certain vaccinations to attend school, unless their parent fills out a government-issued form explaining a moral, religious, or medical exemption. Supporters say these policies capture the "casual refuseniks" - people who aren't particularly opposed to vaccination, but simply don't make the effort to get their child jabbed.

Other places go further. In Germany, parents can be fined if their children aren't jabbed against measles. Under Australia's "no jab, no pay" policy, parents who refuse immunisations are denied certain benefits.

But those tough, coercive policies leave some uncomfortable. "Mandatory vaccination has been steered away from in the UK for good reason," says Hungerford. For one thing, he thinks, "you risk excluding vulnerable people from things like childcare."

Others say that barring unvaccinated children from school is only likely to alienate their parents further from healthcare, amplifying their mistrust of authority.

At the Keighley shopping centre, Bill Graham says he doesn't think a mandatory approach would work in his corner of Yorkshire. "I think it destroys trust. Healthcare in Britain is based on trust. Maybe the trust isn't quite where it was again 10, 15 years ago, but we're not going to build that up by mandating healthcare."

All that said, experts stress that there's still a degree of mystery about Britain's vaccination problem.

Some parents who refuse jabs simply won't say why - and they're the same groups (poor, lower levels of educational attainment) who are hard to reach via surveys.

This becomes apparent towards the end of my morning at the clinic, when a couple in their thirties arrive to have their baby weighed. Hussain quickly notices that their 23-week-old hasn't had any of his recommended jabs - and asks if they might consider it. The couple glance at each other and quietly shake their heads.

They don't give a reason, and they turn down my request for an interview (the only parents who do so).

Still, Hussain hopes their conversation might have planted a seed. "I've sent her some information. Giving them a platform to speak about their concerns can help.

"It's not us forcing it on anyone. This is a choice."

articles.title: 'It can be isolating' - how does hot weather impact anxiety?
articles.summary: Southampton woman Lauren has health anxiety that gets worse during the hot weather.
articles.body:
"When it's hot the air feels different in your lungs. Your brain just starts going, 'Something's different - and therefore bad' even though it's not."

The hot weather and high temperatures can trigger anxiety and other mental health problems, according to new research from Oxford University.

Lauren Murphy, from Southampton, has anxiety and agoraphobia, a disorder defined by an intense fear of feeling trapped.

The heat can trigger this feeling of panic, making her feel "really isolated" and like she cannot breathe.

"You end up overthinking every single sensation, even if it's a regular everyday occurrence," she says.

The 34-year-old has had anxiety for about a decade, but noticed it became worse after she became a parent and was diagnosed with ADHD.

"When you're an anxious person, especially with health anxiety, you're so much more in tune with your body," she says.

Then her anxiety also got worse as the heat got stronger, which she first noticed when she went on holiday abroad a few years ago, and the high temperatures made her feel like she could not breathe.

When similar conditions arrived in the UK, she says those fears returned.

"It really brought it all back. This year has probably been the worst." she said.

A fourth heatwave of the year is affecting parts of the UK , with a drought declared across large parts of England and the whole of Wales.

"Your heart might be beating faster, you're sweating more, and all of that feels so alarming when you're anxious," Lauren says.

She says those physical sensations - including a heavy feeling in her chest, a racing heart and difficulty concentrating - can reinforce the symptoms of anxiety, creating a cycle that is difficult to break.

"It's like anxiety's the main character and you're the ensemble."

Lauren is not alone - a 2022 study from the University of Bath estimated that about 4.6% of people in the UK had climate anxiety.

It is a form of mental distress recognised by professional bodies and the NHS, with young people and women among the groups most at risk, according to a 2025 study .

"Heat stress might feel like anxiety, they have the same physiological response," says Professor Ciara MaCabe, who works at the University of Reading and specialises in mental health.

"So the anxiety feelings are due to the heat, and then anxiety can kick in.

"The more heatwaves we have obviously more and more people are going to experience this."

Lauren says she has since found ways to calm herself when she starts to panic.

"Journaling helps - your mind can think so much faster than you can write. Writing slows everything down," she says.

She says tapping techniques help "ground" her as well as breathing exercises, yoga and being in nature.

Her advice to others experiencing anxiety is to ask for help.

"I always underestimate my ability to cope," she says.

"Being brave isn't the absence of fear. It's having that fear and doing it anyway."

articles.title: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes
articles.summary: The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least £41,700.
articles.body:
More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialist scheme intended for high-earning individuals despite visa rules being tightened, BBC Verify has found.

The Home Office scheme allows registered employers to recruit workers from overseas who meet a certain skill level. The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least £41,700.

But a year on from the rule change, BBC Verify has found more than 1,500 grocery and convenience stores, 150 taxi operators, 100 barber shops, and dozens of car washes and vape shops are still on the register and able to sponsor people to apply for visas.

More than 100 of those businesses were added to the skilled worker sponsorship list after the rules were tightened. Being on the register does not mean applications for individual visas would be approved.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said on Thursday the government will "make sure that the rules are being properly enforced because we cannot have employers getting round the rules or finding different ways to deviate".

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review into the presence of vape shops, barbers and car washes on the skilled worker sponsor register two months ago, following concerns over the "potential misuse of the system". The Home Office said at the time that any businesses seeking to abuse the system would have their licences revoked.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We have raised the skilled worker threshold and over 100 occupations are now ineligible for new skilled worker visas."

It is understood some of the companies that joined the register after the rules changed may have applied before they took effect. Some companies may have also remained on the register because they were approved before July 2025 or are sponsoring workers who were already in the UK.

There are more than 120,000 businesses with licences to sponsor skilled workers. The skilled worker scheme was introduced after Brexit for employers to recruit workers after EU free movement ended. Smaller firms must pay a £611 fee to apply to join the register while larger businesses, such as those with more than 50 staff, pay a fee of £1,682. Anyone can be visited by the UK Visas and Immigration service during the application process.

Until July last year, someone being hired from abroad could qualify for sponsorship if their qualifications met an A-Level or equivalent standard, as long as they were paid at least £38,700 in most cases. Since the rule change, non-graduate professions, such as shop managers, are no longer eligible to apply. There are also higher English-language skill requirements that were introduced in January this year.

The Home Office said there were 68,067 skilled worker visas granted in the 12 months to March this year - 29,745 to main applicants and 38,322 to their dependants - which is 30% lower than the year before. IT professionals were the most common type of people to be granted the visas, followed by those people working in finance, while the fall in approvals was mostly attributed to those in food preparation and hospitality trades no longer qualifying for the scheme.

Jobs including sales and retail assistants, taxi drivers and chauffeurs are currently listed by the government as ineligible for skilled worker visas, but there are some exemptions, such as bricklayers, carpenters or nursing assistants and other occupations where there is a shortage in the UK.

The Home Office revoked 3,299 licences in 2025 compared with 347 in 2023. Its register does not state how many certificates of sponsorship or visas have been issued for each business or what type of role it has hired for, but Home Office guidance states firms must offer genuine jobs that meet skill and salary rules, and only sponsor workers for eligible roles.

As businesses are only listed by name, it is not always clear what industry a company operates within. BBC Verify identified the more than 1,900 small high-street businesses that had retained a sponsorship licence by matching their names and locations to Companies House records and Google business listings to identify whether the mini marts, car washes and other small operations were on the list, and by analysing company names.

Around 1,700 of those were in England, more than 140 were in Scotland, over 80 were in Wales and just two were in Northern Ireland.

Separately, BBC Verify found 60 businesses on the register that had been fined for employing illegal workers between April 2024 and December 2025. They had been fined a combined £2.5m.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "Illegal working will not be accepted, and businesses who face two or more illegal working penalties of up to £60,000, or fail to pay a penalty the first time, will have their license to hire workers revoked."

Speaking about the visa rule change, Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, said that if businesses were on the register before the rules changed, they can continue to employ people they had already sponsored. "But they can't now bring in a new person to do those jobs."

Toby Way, a lawyer at WestBridge Business Immigration which helps businesses apply to be sponsors, told BBC Verify that while most sponsorship approvals are legitimate, "We come across a lot of exaggeration and some downright lying about sponsored roles".

"Hotels and restaurants have been hit massively by the rule changes. They're now unable to sponsor a chef or a manager, but they might claim they need someone for marketing or book-keeping, because those roles are on the temporary shortage list," he said.

"We know the Home Office looks at the finances of the businesses now and whether their revenue or profit means they can pay the required salary."

Immigration lawyer Joanna Hunt of DAC Beachcroft said that it would be difficult for a high street shop to justify sponsorship at the degree level.

"Subject to a few exceptions, a job needs to be skilled to 'degree level' to allow a business to sponsor a worker to fill it and the Home Office will consider if the role fits with the type of business the sponsor operates. A high street shop may find this requirement difficult to demonstrate."

Additional reporting by Rob England and Libby Rogers

articles.title: Why have obesity rates doubled since 1993?
articles.summary: Around seven million more adults are living with obesity than would have been if obesity rates had stayed the same as 1993.
articles.body:
If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.

There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.

It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?

According to new analysis by the King's Fund, in 1993 15% of those aged 16 and over in England were obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.

Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.

Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.

"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.

There are several factors behind the rise in obesity, including changes in eating habits and food prices over the last 30 years.

Service industry - or "white collar" jobs - take a larger share of the economy and there has been a decline in traditional manufacturing and other "blue collar" work such as manual labour.

This means more people are in sedentary office jobs so spend more time sitting down than moving around.

Food prices have also fallen since the 1990s, partly because of increased competition between the major supermarkets alongside an increase in fast food outlets and home delivery.

Buck told the BBC that these changes mean it's "far easier to over-consume or consume in ways that add to our weight".

"With things like deliveries, it's very easy and convenient now to click a button and you get a takeaway at your door, so we're making it much easier to have high fat, high salt and high sugar foods."

Takeaways high in fats, salt and sugar are more widely available in areas of high deprivation where people are at higher risk of obesity.

Less healthy foods in supermarkets are also cheaper than they were three decades ago, while there have been several cost-of-living crises in recent years.

What has the government tried to do about it?

Obesity can be a risk factor for several chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, osteoarthritis and some cancers.

Reports estimate obesity and being overweight costs the UK economy approximately £126bn per year, including £12bn to the NHS - roughly 7% of its annual budget.

Since 1992 - the year before data on obesity in England was first collected - 14 national obesity strategies have been published.

Campaigners argue progress has been too slow and calls for further intervention have increased in recent years.

Tony Blair's government introduced a ban on junk food advertising during children's TV programmes - although some campaigners were calling for a wider ban - while Gordon Brown launched a strategy aiming to reverse the "rising tide of obesity" after becoming prime minister in 2007.

The Conservative government introduced a UK-wide levy on high-sugar soft drinks in 2018, causing several manufacturers to cut sugar levels in their products so that they fell below the levy threshold.

During his final weeks in office in 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron considered banning "buy one get one free" deals for unhealthy products in supermarkets and restricting TV ads for junk food and other high sugar products.

Although both Theresa May and Boris Johnson argued at times for further action, Cameron's ideas were not followed up, partly due to the pandemic which delayed plans further, and afterwards when ministers argued restrictions on such deals would be unfair on shoppers due to surging inflation.

In January this year, the Labour government introduced a ban on junk food advertising before 21:00 on television and at any time online after almost a decade of consideration.

Further plans to crack down on the sale of unhealthy food items are still yet to come into effect despite being first pledged by Labour in 2024, while a recent select committee report urged ministers to do more like stopping fast food outlets opening close to schools.

Weight loss drugs such as GLP1s are increasingly being used to treat obesity, though only adults with a BMI of at least 35 and who have at least one pre-existing weight-related health condition qualify for Wegovy on the NHS.

People with cardiovascular disease who are classed as overweight, but not quite obese, can also be given the drug, while Mounjaro has been available from specialist NHS weight-loss clinics in England and Wales since March 2025.

Many people chose to buy these drugs privately.

A new weight loss pill from Wegovy is now available to buy privately from High Street and online pharmacies in the UK - but is not yet on the NHS.

The Department of Health and Social Care says weight loss jabs are only one part of a broader plan.

It says tackling the promotion of less healthy food and drink, increasing exercise and encouraging people to eat healthier options are all important for addressing obesity.

Earlier this year , England's Chief Medical Officer Prof Sir Chris Whitty said it would be a "societal failure" if medicating people for life was our only answer to obesity.

He says the lessons are there in other countries, such as France, which have kept obesity levels stable.

Now the question is what do we want to learn?

articles.title: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men
articles.summary: Women can make higher returns but only about a quarter of UK women have investments, compared with about 40% of men.
articles.body:
Women who invest their money get slightly higher long-term returns than men, new analysis suggests.

But only about a quarter of UK women have investments, compared with about 40% of men, a separate report shows.

We've looked at the data behind these trends, which reveal some surprising differences in how men and women approach investing.

Teleri Evans was 25 when she began saving into a Help To Buy ISA then a couple of years later she took out a stocks and shares Lifetime ISA. By 33, she had £40,000 saved - with £8,000 of it returns on her investments.

"I saved aggressively, and lived at my mum's for half of that time, so I could save as close as possible to the maximum £4,000 per year into Lifetime ISA," she says.

The civil servant from Cardiff used the money towards a house deposit earlier this year with her partner.

Only 26% of UK women invest, but that this falls to 23% for those under 45, according to a study by consumer finance website Boring Money.

In contrast, 41% of all men invest, which holds steady at 40% of those under 45.

So why are fewer women investing than men?

It can be "largely attributed to culture", according to Gillian Fleming, co-founder and managing director of UK-based Mint Ventures, a women-led angel investment firm.

"Men historically have been more likely to make family investment decisions, and women have also historically not owned the balance of wealth, but that is changing now," she says.

"Also, money and wealth creation is not a topic that women often discuss, and we would like to change that."

Teleri says she has noticed a shift of late. "Investing is definitely something that women are talking about more, which is always a good thing," she says. "That's the case with my friendship group."

When women do invest in stocks and shares, analysis by Fidelity International found that over three years its female personal investing customers recorded cumulative returns of 50%, compared with 47% for men. The analysis does not identify the reason for the difference, but why may it be the case?

One possible clue to women's slightly higher long-term returns lies in how often they buy and sell their investments, with Barclays data showing that women trade around half as frequently as men.

This could be because women are more patient and risk averse, says Joanna Floyd, business psychologist at London-based The Work Psychologists.

"Studies show that male investors trade more than women, chasing higher returns, but women actually get higher returns," she says.

"The restraint that keeps women out of the market in the first place is the very same thing that rewards them once they are in it."

That more cautious approach to risk can be seen beyond investing, with women more likely to choose certainty when faced with a financial gamble.

When it comes to how women invest, Fleming says they are deliberately more cautious.

"Women are often accused of being more risk adverse, we call it more risk aware," she says. "Certainly from speaking to male investors their main focus is on the rate of return."

Fleming also says women appear to invest more broadly. "Men are more likely to invest in technology companies for their higher potential returns, whereas women want to invest in a broader range, from retail to food and drink, health and beauty, fem tech and creative industries."

Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at financial services company Hargreaves Lansdown, agrees that women choose the companies they invest in carefully.

"Women appear to place relatively greater weight on where their money is going and what impact it might have, as well as the reassurance that an investment is right for them," she says.

"Our research suggests men are...more readily attracted by the potential financial return."

Jemma Slingo, pensions and investment specialist at investment firm Fidelity International, says female investors "appear more likely to connect investing with real-life goals, from building emergency savings to looking after children."

It's important to remember women in the UK generally have less money to invest than men because the continuing gender pay gap means they earn less on average.

Macdonald says that the investment sector "needs to do a better job of making investing feel accessible, relevant and connected to people's own goals and values".

"Addressing this would be good for women's long-term financial resilience and for the UK economy."

articles.title: Where does this unorthodox by-election victory leave Nigel Farage?
articles.summary: As expected, the Reform UK leader easily won the Clacton by-election but was nowhere to be seen after the result.
articles.body:
The Clacton by-election has been unorthodox from the start – and results day has been no different, with winning candidate Nigel Farage choosing not to turn up to the result of a contest he himself triggered.

Not only that - I got up this morning anticipating being in the audience, on your behalf, for a Farage victory speech, here in Clacton, and then doing an interview with him afterwards.

Neither of those things have happened. The Reform UK leader cancelled all of the interviews he had planned, with the BBC and others.

He said his no show at the declaration, in the Clacton Leisure Centre, was because the police had warned him of an attempt to "disrupt and degrade the result" and he did not want to be "demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".

His aides emphasise too his ongoing, deeply held worries about his security.

It is also true that by vanishing rather than publicly celebrating his win he has avoided, for now at least, all of the questions about Reform's finances that led to the by-election in the first place.

Instead, the focus has been on his victory and the oddities of the race and its aftermath.

Farage's team point out he got more votes in this contest than he did two years ago at the general election, even though it was pretty clear all along that he would win.

And for a by-election in mid summer, there was a decent turn out too, of 44%, which suggests many people locally took the contest seriously.

Speaking to folk in Walton-on-the-Naze and in Clacton-on-Sea today, there is no doubt Farage has his vociferous local critics, but plenty do share Reform's view that this result matters far more than the resumption of the investigation by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards.

"We consider this matter closed," is how one aide put it to me, punchily.

Except, of course, it isn't - the commissioner's inquiry is up and running again and Farage is likely to be interviewed by him in the coming weeks.

Farage faces renewed watchdog probe after Clacton by-election victory

Farage's by-election victory won't stop questions about finances

Count Binface gets almost 10,000 votes in Clacton by-election

What do Nigel Farage's constituents think of his re-election?

It is a question prompting at least some debate within the party.

"When he goes down this angry route he doesn't help himself," the prominent Reform activist Tim Montgomerie told Radio 4's The World At One.

Montgomerie, the founder of the ConservativeHome website, defected to Reform two years ago. He praised Farage's political ability but added: "It's very frustrating how he's behaved today. He needs to get a grip of this problem."

Montgomerie argued Farage and Reform were at their best when they were more positive rather than "inward looking" and focused on "grievances."

The "grievances," as Montgomerie puts it, are real and legitimate, say Farage's friends.

In the short term at least and from a point of weakness I have previously written about , the by-election allowed Farage to get on the front foot and to frame an argument, as he saw it, as the people versus those out to get him.

Rubbish, say his critics, the rules apply to all MPs and the undeclared £5m gift from the billionaire businessman Christopher Harborne, in the months before Farage became an MP, should have been registered, they insist.

Talking to GB News in the early hours of this morning, before the result, Farage repeated a concession, of sorts, about this: "If I made one sin, it's that I haven't filled in a piece of paper.

"I've broken no law, I've broken no tax law, I've taken no public money. I don't even own a motor home. Maybe I haven't filled in a piece of paper. I'm confident I'm right - we'll see where we go."

He has long maintained he sought legal advice about whether he needed to declare the money and had been told he didn't.

The wider question is where Nigel Farage and Reform find themselves in the big picture politically and whether their current approach is a wise one.

There is early evidence of something of a Burnham bounce for Labour, which has disrupted Reform's long standing lead in the opinion polls.

And the Conservatives appear more chipper and competitive than a year ago too.

Then there is the rise of Restore Britain, run by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

Let's be clear: none of the political parties are wildly popular at the moment, but Reform's support has shrivelled a bit and their rivals are more upbeat.

The landscape for the new political season at Westminster is taking shape, ahead of MPs returning to the Commons in a few weeks.

Labour with a spring in its step, for now at least. Reform punchy but feeling under the cosh and plenty of the others scrapping for attention too.

It will be a fascinating few months ahead.

images.caption: Nigel Farage did not attend the declaration of the result in Clacton

articles.title: Who voted for Count Binface in the Clacton by-election and why?
articles.summary: Cheaper Flakes and using Adele to fund the NHS - voters on why they support a man dressed as a bin.
articles.body:
Self-styled intergalactic space warrior Count Binface finished second in the Clacton by-election on Thursday with 9,455 votes.

A record 34 candidates stood in the contest, but Binface and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage were the only contenders to secure more than 500 votes.

The other major UK parties boycotted the election, which was triggered by Farage's resignation as an MP in July, having won the seat from the Conservatives in 2024.

Binface has stood in various high-profile elections around the country in recent years. Before Clacton, his best results were more than 24,000 votes in the last two London mayoral elections.

With more candidates on the ballot than ever before, why did 26.9% of voters choose a man wearing a bin on his head?

First-time voter Ben Peters, 18, from Holland-on-Sea, said the election had been a "joke" since the start.

He said: "It was a bit of a thrill, but at the same time it felt almost pointless because I knew that, no matter what I did, Farage was going to get back into the seat."

Binface's policies had included nationalising the singer Adele, moving a pub hand dryer in Uxbridge and enforcing a 99p price tag on ice creams with 99 flakes.

Peters said: "Even if it means voting for Count Binface and getting 99p ice creams for 99 flakes, that is one more step than Nigel Farage has ever done for Clacton."

Alex Greenwood, from Thorpe-le-Soken, acknowledged some policies were "a bit silly" but the 18-year-old student argued there was an underlying logic to them.

"Nationalising Adele... all of Adele's song proceeds go to a private company which goes to shareholders and her songs are pretty much cultural icons," he said.

"It's not actually that far-fetched... why not have all that money go to the government which could be used on the NHS and stuff?"

Greenwood suggested his vote was partially a protest against Farage, whom he believes called the by-election to avoid scrutiny from the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards .

He added: "I do like Binface. I don't like Farage all that much."

Before Farage quit his Clacton seat in July, Parliament's standards watchdog had been investigating him for not declaring a £5m gift he received from billionaire Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne before he became an MP.

He said the by-election was a "people versus the establishment" showdown, saying the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions".

Kerry Mitchell, who lives in Wix, said she had voted for Count Binface because he would have made for a "more credible, honest, responsible, not to say committed, MP than Nigel Farage".

The 61-year-old, who voted Labour in 2024, said: "Nigel Farage poses a real threat to democracy in the UK and if Binface had won, it would have put an end to him.

"And it also added some much-needed humour and lightness into politics.

"The world is in a very dark place at the moment, and a bit of levity and humour is fantastic, especially when you contrast it with the rhetoric of outrage, division and anger that we hear from the far-right."

Tracey Donovan, 61, also voted Labour in the last general election and decided to back Binface on Thursday because it was "the only viable alternative to Farage".

"I detest Farage and everything he stands for. He has done absolutely nothing for our constituency," she told the BBC.

"I want an MP who represents our area with the constituents' interests being addressed.

"He claims the establishment is against him, but he is the establishment."

Donovan, who has lived in Clacton her entire life, added she was pleasantly surprised by how many people voted for Binface.

"He had almost a third of the votes cast as supposedly a joke candidate, and I'm very pleased that it is only really just over a quarter of the constituency [voting] population who actively backed Farage and Reform," she said.

"Count Binface could have rid this town of its Little Britain label if more of the 55% who didn't vote at all had got out there and voted against Farage."

Salon owner Verda Rigby, who lives in St Osyth, used to vote for the Conservatives before she "became a socialist" and started supporting Labour.

In this election, however, as voting for Labour was not an option, the 66-year-old instead opted for Binface.

"I could have stayed at home, but we fought for the right to vote and, look, it was partly for the joke that Farage is," she said.

"And I despise the right-wing parties Reform, Restore, and Reclaim - it's like a bad pop group of numpties."

Philip Bird, 66, has lived in Clacton for 30 years and said he, too, would have voted for Labour if the party had stood a candidate in the election.

"I think it was absolutely right not to stand anyone because none of the major parties should have condoned this election," he said.

"It was farcical, completely unnecessary, and designed to distract attention, and it wasn't going to change anything, so I was quite comfortable voting for a satirical candidate.

"Farage has greatly harmed the conversation in this country, he has been a dreadful MP, he has done nothing for Clacton, and in reality his politics are precisely what Clacton doesn't need."

In a statement after his win on Friday , the Reform leader said: "The verdict is now in, and it is a convincing, overwhelming win, with more votes than we got in the general election of 2024.

"Today, the voters in Clacton have stuck up two fingers to the entire political establishment."

articles.title: Solar eclipse in the South West: Pac-man to Shinto myths
articles.summary: Thousands turned out to watch the solar eclipse in the South West; here's what they made of it.
articles.body:
People across the South West gathered to watch a rare solar eclipse on Wednesday evening.

The event began at approx 19:00 BST with the Moon passing between the Earth and the Sun, creating a crescent shape in the sky.

In Sidmouth, families gathered to watch the event, with children describing it as a "once in a lifetime opportunity" and others comparing the shape of the Sun to a banana.

One young girl, Charlotte, said: "It's really exciting because the next time I'll see one, I'll be a lot older. It's like a once in a lifetime opportunity."

Charlie described the atmosphere as "magical", and said: "The kids haven't stopped screaming and been dancing around since we've been here."

Some people marked birthdays and anniversaries during the eclipse, giving the evening a romantic significance.

One young girl named Alice described the eclipse as brilliant, and said: "It kind of looks like Pac-man", whilst another felt that the sun disappearing was "kind of scary".

Commander Dave Lee, Royal Navy Parachute Display Team, spent the event parachuting into Pendennis Castle at the beginning of the eclipse.

Lee was one of five members of the Royal Navy and Royal Marines jumping out of the small aircraft at about 6,000ft (1829m), before deploying their colourful canopies.

Lee said: "It is really a once in a lifetime experience, you have a very real feeling of immediacy and freedom, and you get a great view."

David Heathfield spent the event telling stories about the "rare" mythology surrounding eclipses, in particular, the story of Amano-Iwato - the Japanese goddess of the sun - who hid in a cave depriving the world of light.

"I had to go all the way to Japanese Shinto mythology to find it", he said.

In Cornwall, people gathered at locations including Bude and a stone circle on the moors, with one person describing the experience as "very strange" and "surreal".

Another person said: "I think it's very, very spiritual."

In West Penwith, Mark said wildlife appeared to react to the changing light, with birds returning to their roosts as the eclipse took place.

"All the birds have gone to bed," he said, adding that a flock of seagulls and choughs had been feeding on flying ants shortly before they returned to the cliffs.
