articles.title: The dangers of politicians being "too online" - or not online enough
articles.summary: In an era when reputations can be made or broken with a single post, getting the balance right is tricky.
articles.body:
In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal".

It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election.

This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years".

More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. The government has spent the last few weeks recruiting producers, videographers and strategists, working out of both Whitehall and No 10 North in Manchester.

In his first month as PM, Burnham posted more than 50 times on Instagram, ranging from meetings with world leaders, campaigners, farmers and influencers, to meme-based content like ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey as part of an announcement on business rates. Strategists believe Instagram and TikTok can play to Burnham's communication strengths and sense of humour.

They're all at it, of course. Videos of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch tearing into the budget or mocking ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer have gone viral. Reform UK's Nigel Farage has by far the biggest online audience of any UK party leader, with 7.6 million followers across Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube.

In Scotland, the SNP have long mobilised their online army to campaign for independence, building a following larger than that of the Lib Dems, which campaigns across Britain, whose leader Ed Davey has achieved some success with campaign stunts going viral.

Restore Britain, founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe, enjoys its highest level of support among users of X. The platform is owned by Elon Musk who has publicly endorsed the party, expanding its reach.

Plaid Cymru, newly installed in government in Wales, is still experimenting with its approach, using First Minister Rhun Ap Iorweth in "fun" memes while also posting more serious interview excerpts. The Greens' Zack Polanski has made much of running his own accounts, though as he has found in recent weeks, this comes with risks too.

So how much is enough? In a world where reputations can be made (or broken) with one comment or collaboration, getting the balance right is tricky – being accessible, authentic and approachable, without being cringe. And does it make any difference to elections?

Cameron's successor, Theresa May, was similarly doubtful about the merits of social media. When she took office she rebuffed aides who suggested she start tweeting: "People don't say 'pass me the hashtag newspaper, or I'd like a hashtag coffee'." Announcements were to be made formally. When cabinet ministers were appointed in May's first reshuffle, it was heralded in press statements beneath the UK government coat of arms.

By contrast, this summer, presenting my 5 Live show from Downing Street during Burnham's first reshuffle, I could predict the appearance of another new minister because the two-person social media team from No 10 would move into position to capture the new arrivals on their cameras.

Of course, prime ministers (and wannabes) have long adapted to new technology. Winston Churchill harnessed the power of radio, but thought television a vulgar diversion. In the 1960s, Labour's Harold Wilson modelled his TV campaigning on JFK in America. In the 1990s, and 2000s leaders like Tony Blair were just as likely to be found on the chatshow sofa as on the Today programme.

Now, podcasts give long-form - and less combative - opportunities to connect with voters, while social media gives a quick hit of direct democratic dopamine.

Peter Hyman, a former adviser to both Tony Blair and Keir Starmer when in Downing Street, said the success of Burnham's early digital output was about "quantity as well as quality".

"You have to narrate the story of what you are doing three or four or five times a day so that you are out there regularly," Hyman said. "Keir Starmer wasn't out there enough and therefore it wasn't landing."

There is a causality dilemma here. Is Burnham more popular in the polls because he is racking up the likes on social media, or is he doing better online because people like him?

Not everyone is convinced. Cody Dahler, a comedian who posts sweary political explainers to his two million followers, warns voters will become cynical if they sense politicians are just using social media simply "as a comms tool". Burnham, Dahler told me on Newsnight, comes across like a "cool substitute teacher".

And after Burnham released a video discussing what a bread roll is called in different parts of the country – barm, cob or bap - to promote his plans for devolution, broadcaster Piers Morgan asked him to "stop wasting your time and ours with these cringe videos".

And therein lies the difficulty of striking a balance. Bea Timpson, a former press secretary to Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak who says she prefers "trad media" like broadcast and print, added: "I have to accept that it's now non-negotiable to be online a bit, but you definitely can be too much."

TV and online websites remain the most used sources for news, but more and more of us say we also get news from social media, according to media watchdog Ofcom. While this is highest among 16-24 year olds at 78%, a majority of adults in every age group use social media to access news, apart from the over-65s. Even among over 75s, 22% find out what is happening in the world from social media. For politicians, this is no longer just about reaching young people – this is all voters.

Some platforms are more important than others. Even after Elon Musk's conversion of Twitter into X, you will still see MPs, spin doctors and journalists in the Westminster village scrolling through the platform, but digital strategists say "real voters" are found on other platforms. The main parties have far more followers on Facebook (four million combined), which is much more widely used overall, than X (where they have a combined 3.2 million).

Politicians have always looked abroad for policy and campaigning ideas, and social media is no different.

Those on the right seek to emulate the impact Donald Trump has on TruthSocial, while left-wing politicians look to the success of Zohran Mamdani becoming mayor of New York.

Some have even imported social media experts from overseas. In 2019 Boris Johnson hired New Zealand duo Ben Guerin and Sean Topham to run the digital campaign for the general election. They imported into UK politics the concept of "shitposting", releasing deliberately bad images in order to generate a reaction. This included posting a tweet featuring the slogan "Get Brexit Done" in Comic Sans, a font loathed by graphic designers.

There was a method in the madness. "People are more likely to engage with something if they feel like it's been written by a human, not by a committee of design experts," Guerin told me. "It's pretty easy to go viral for doing something weird and wacky, but that doesn't always advance the objectives of your campaign."

This seems to be borne out by some recent hits. Burnham's TikTok post rating pub snacks attracted a million views. Yet a less gimmicky video, straightforwardly listing the five things he said he had done in his first week as PM, got five million.

There is an inherent tension in political social media. Authenticity is key. Yet who really expects the prime minister to be shooting and uploading his own content?

Back in 2013 I wrote a story about how Cameron's Twitter account had favourited a tweet mocking William Hague from an account handle that made a crude joke about former Tory MP Norman Tebbit being injured in the Brighton bombing.

The prime minister's director of communications called me to complain about my "slapdash and crappy" reporting. My crime? Including a sentence which allowed for the possibility that someone other than Cameron had clicked on the like button by mistake. This would, apparently, spoil the magic for those that thought the prime minister was running his own account for his 500,000 followers.

We now know that Zack Polanski does indeed have his own log-ins. The leader of the Green Party in England and Wales faced criticism in May for sharing a post condemning police actions in the Golders Green attack, for which he apologised. Then in July he accepted an Instagram collaboration which included a man wearing a T-shirt featuring a cartoon guillotine and the song lyrics "we're only making plans for Nigel". Reform UK said it amounted to incitement of violence against Farage. "I'm accepting my responsibility in that I shouldn't have accepted that collaboration," Polanski said, but refused to apologise.

Reform UK's Gawain Towler, a long-time media adviser to Nigel Farage, says: " My big takeaway is: don't be a berk on social media, which I think was Zack Polanski's big takeaway too."

Dov Forman, who helped Tory-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick grow his following from 20,000 to more than half a million with viral clips including confronting fare dodgers on the London Underground, says it is "risky" for a leader to run their own social media. But sometimes it can be a risk worth taking.

Badenoch has taken to directing her own videos, telling aides what she wants to post. She has attracted backing on X from American rappers Nicki Minaj and Azealia Banks. Those are the sort of authentic third-party endorsements politicians crave.

On the day he became prime minister, a video was released of Burnham being interviewed on the Career Ladder, a series run by Ukrainian TikToker Max Klymenko who interviews guests about their career, while standing on a ladder. "If they personally haven't seen the channel it's sometimes quite difficult to make sense for them," Klymenko says. Burnham had seen the show, and did use the ladder.

Which leads us to the big question: Does any of this actually work? Emma Connolly, an academic who has researched this at the Digital Speech Lab at UCL, isn't sure. "We don't necessarily have really strong evidence or convincing evidence that it could really persuade or transform the opinion of opponent voters or even those that are undecided," she says.

Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?

Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise

And this in turn raises the question of how long the Burnham digital honeymoon might last. Can a prime minister TikTok his way through a war, terror attack or controversial court case? Announcing a new giveaway may go viral, but what about the details of the cuts to pay for it?

The truth is none of this is new, as Hyman explains: "The politicians who get this wrong think that social media is now the only place to be, and a substitute for doing the hard work and the heavy lifting of actually getting the right policy, getting the right narrative, and telling that story properly," he says. "Politics is about winning arguments."

After all, politicians have always wanted to be liked. It's just these days they can see it instantly if you hit that heart button on your feed.

Listen to Matt Chorley live from Westminster, weekdays from 14:00 on BBC Radio 5 Live.

articles.title: Is Vine back? Short-form video-sharing app Divine opens to public
articles.summary: The app lets users create six-second looping videos and hosts more than two million classic videos.
articles.body:
A new app seen as a spiritual successor to short-form video service Vine has been released to the public.

Much like the original, Divine lets users create and share videos which are just six seconds long and repeat on a loop.

The new app also hosts more than two million original Vine videos and - in a bid to further distance itself from other platforms - bans content made by AI.

Divine's founder, former Twitter employee Evan Henshaw-Plath, told the BBC he wanted to create the app because he felt social media needed "a reset".

"I want to see it rival other apps because I think we have gone awry," he said in an interview a few weeks before the public launch.

He said it was important that there was no AI-generated content on Divine, adding he was "sick and tired of seeing videos and not knowing whether it was real".

"I want to be able to have fun and not have to second guess these things," he said.

At its peak, Vine had more than 200 million monthly active users and helped launch the careers of some of the internet's biggest stars.

Jake Paul and Lele Pons are two of those who made their names on the platform before it was shut down by its owner Twitter in 2017.

Divine is backed by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, who had a senior role at the social media platform when it purchased the Vine in 2012.

It is built on a decentralised system called Nostr, meaning it is not controlled by a single company in the same way as platforms such as TikTok or Instagram.

This means users can potentially take their accounts and content with them to other services that use the same system, rather than being locked into one platform.

A similar approach has been used by X rivals Bluesky and Mastodon.

Divine's website FAQs outlines several ways for the platform to ensure all videos on the app are human-made, without AI involvement.

For example, users have to record videos live in the app, rather than uploading from elsewhere, and it will use a verification tool called ProofMode - which works like a digital receipt for a piece of media.

When users record something using a device with ProofMode, it can attach information which helps verify elements such as when it was recorded and whether the file has been altered since.

Users will also be able to flag suspected AI content, and automated systems as well as humans will be involved in looking for signs of the tech.

Divine's attempt to do things differently could also be its biggest challenge, according to social media analyst Matt Navarra.

"The mechanisms people dislike about modern social media are often the same that made those platforms extraordinarily good at keeping people there," he said.

"So Divine now has to prove you can remove some of the addiction without removing the magic."

Aside from its new content and features, the treasure trove of old Vines created by some of the platform's biggest stars could well be a draw for those who remember their first time around (and around).

Henshaw-Plath said he initially set out to simply recreate Vine's short-video format, but then wondered if he could bring back its old videos too.

He discovered the Internet Archive had preserved a copy of Vine's data and spent months reconstructing it.

"I was like, oh, this is really cool," he said, initially expecting only a few thousand people to be interested.

Instead, 10,000 people installed the app within its first few hours, overwhelming its servers.

"That's when I went, oh, there's something more here," he said.

As to why people may still have interest in short-form content when many apps such as YouTube and TikTok have moved towards much longer videos, he compared Vine's format to the haiku.

"Yet poetry is a form in which we value and which has meaning. And so there's many ways in which Vine was poetry."

The challenge for Divine is to turn that nostalgia into something that works for a new generation of social media users.

articles.title: Starmer donates biography of himself to Downing Street library
articles.summary: The former PM and seven of his ministers have added to the collection, which began in 1931.
articles.body:
A book about the life of Sir Keir Starmer has become the newest addition to the Downing Street library, after being donated by Sir Keir himself.

Keir Starmer: The Biography, written by journalist and former Labour adviser Tom Baldwin, has now joined the collection of more than 400 books, some of which are kept in two bookcases in Downing Street's Cabinet Room.

The library was established in 1931 by the first Labour Prime Minister, Ramsay MacDonald, and since then prime ministers and ministers have been invited to make contributions.

Seven ministers who served in Sir Keir's government have also added books to the shelves.

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves added her own book, Alice in Westminster: The political life of Alice Bacon

Darren Jones, who served as a senior minister between 2024 and 2026, gave Laudato Si: On Care for our Common Home - a book by Pope Francis which calls for greater protection of the environment

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy offered her book All In: How we build a country that works

Nick Thomas-Symonds, a Cabinet Office minister in the last government, also chose his own book - a biography of former Labour Prime Minister Harold Wilson

Women and Equalities minister Bridget Phillipson picked Choose Freedom: The Future for Democratic Socialism by former Labour deputy leader Roy Hattersley

Former Wales Secretary Jo Stevens gave The Fed: a history of the South Wales miners in the twentieth century by Hywel Francis and David Smith

Treasury minister James Murray donated Instruction to Deliver - a book by Sir Michael Barber about his experience being a civil servant in Tony Blair's government

As Labour leader, Sir Keir did not appear to be much of a reader. In one interview in 2024, he struggled to name a favourite novel and when he appeared on Radio 4's Desert Island Discs he picked an atlas as the book he would take with him.

In contrast, his successor Andy Burnham, an English Literature graduate, has spoken of his fondness for poetry, in particular the works of Tony Harrison and Philip Larkin.

He is unlikely to donate a volume to the library at this early stage of his premiership, but if he finds time to peruse the shelves, he will find an eclectic collection.

Unsurprisingly there are weighty tomes about politics, philosophy, history, religion - The Law and Custom of the Constitution (3 Vols), The Rhetoric of Aristotle - A Translation, An Analytical Concordance to The Holy Bible.

Many ministers have donated their own publications – Winston Churchill offered his history book, The World Crisis, 1911-18. Clement Attlee provided Purpose and Policy – a selection of his speeches. Margaret Thatcher gave her memoir The Downing Street Years .

Other prime ministers' choices reflect their own personal passions – Ted Heath donated books about music and sailing. Keen reader Harold Macmillan gave a collection of Rudyard Kipling books.

Desperate prime ministers in need of miracle solutions may be tempted to turn to Magic Symbols of the World written by Pearl Binder, donated by her husband Frederick Elwyn-Jones.

Those looking for a bit of escapism could take a look at The Charm of Birds (donated by Foreign Secretary Edward Grey), Sea Songs (Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine) or The Book of French Wines (Chancellor Geoffrey Howe).

Iain MacLeod, a Conservative minister, provided his own book: Bridge is an Easy Game. According to the Times, he added an inscription: "Perhaps this is the only book in this library which will bring true profit to its readers".

Not all donations make it to the bookcases but instead are kept in storage in the bowels of Downing Street.

Politics Professor Clement Macintyre from Adelaide University, has researched the library extensively.

He says that prior to the 1930s there were not that many books in Downing Street and that one prime minister, Stanley Baldwin, used to send his staff to the nearest library to check facts and quotes.

Prof Macintyre says the lack of books particularly affected Ramsay MacDonald, the first Labour prime minister.

Unlike many of his prime ministerial predecessors MacDonald - the son of a farm labourer and housemaid - was not independently wealthy and had less money than others to furnish the Downing Street flat.

In 1931, he wrote to cabinet ministers, past and present, asking them to donate a book that was "in some way special or politically significant to them".

Enthusiasm for growing the library has waxed and waned over the years. After a few quiet years, Boris Johnson revived the tradition.

He donated his own book: The Churchill Factor: How one man made history.

Sir Mark Spencer chose Diddly Squat , Jeremy Clarkson's book on running a farm.

Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was an enthusiastic reader of Jilly Cooper novels but does not appear to have donated any of her bonkbusters to the collection.

articles.title: Ofcom investigating Sky News over Farage harassment claims
articles.summary: The Reform UK leader has accused Sky News of sending reporters to a house where his adult daughter lives.
articles.body:
Regulator Ofcom has launched an investigation into Sky News over claims of harassment made by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Last month, Farage accused the broadcaster of infringing his family's privacy by sending reporters to a house where his adult daughter was living.

Reform UK made an official complaint to Ofcom, and called on Sky News to apologise on air and undertake not to seek to contact Farage's family at their homes.

In a post on Facebook on Friday, the Clacton MP said Ofcom was now investigating and that he was "appalled at the way various members of my family have been treated".

The broadcaster denied approaching Farage's daughter when he initially made the allegation.

Chris Mason: Farage attempts to seize back the agenda after finance row

Ofcom would not comment on any investigation but said it treated complaints in strict confidence and would not "publicly confirm the identities of individuals concerned".

Farage claims reporters from Sky News approached his daughter's home while he was out of the country.

Sky News says it did not interact with his daughter, and was trying to ask Farage about a £5m gift he received from cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne before he entered Parliament in July 2024.

A parliamentary standards investigation into whether the gift broke any rules resumed earlier this month after Farage was re-elected as MP for Clacton following a by-election he triggered that was boycotted by the other major parties.

Upon returning to the country, Farage was questioned by Sky News over the undeclared gift, to which he responded: "You tell your bosses, you harass my family any more, there will be serious consequences, that's what your organisation has done this morning, now go away."

When pressed on the donation again, he said: "Did you not hear me? You have broken all the rules, Leveson and everything else, cut."

At the time, Sky News said in a post on X: "Sky News was not at the property at 7.41am. As has already been acknowledged, and as shown in the footage from 10.19am, Sky News was outside a property where Mr Farage was registered to vote at the last election.

"Sky News did not interact with Mr Farage's daughter.

"On a single occasion, we approached the property without a camera operator, identified ourselves as Sky News and the adult occupant chose not to engage. We were seeking to contact Mr Farage to ask questions about the gift he accepted from Mr Cottrell.

"This is a well-established and routine journalistic practice when reporting on matters of legitimate public interest.

"The footage clearly demonstrates that Sky News did not 'hound' or pursue Mr Farage's daughter.

"At no stage did we seek to speak to anyone other than Mr Farage in connection with this story."

The BBC has contacted Sky News for comment.

Ofcom says it aims to conclude fairness and privacy complaints within 90 working days.

articles.title: TikTok to pay $400m to US in one of largest child privacy settlements
articles.summary: The deal stems from a 2024 lawsuit alleging TikTok and its parent company ByteDance collected "vast amounts of data" on millions of users under the age of 13.
articles.body:
TikTok has agreed to pay $400m (£293m) to the US to end a lawsuit alleging its platform violated children‘s privacy, marking one of the largest ever settlements over the issue.

The deal stems from a 2024 suit by the Department of Justice under former President Joe Biden alleging TikTok and its parent company ByteDance collected "vast amounts of data" on millions of users under the age of 13.

Doing so was against the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), a federal law enacted in 2000. It is the same law that dozens of US states are now suing Meta over .

"Children and parents are better protected today than they were when this case began," assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said.

Other companies to have paid penalties to the US government for COPPA violations include Google's YouTube, which in 2019 paid $170m, and Epic Games, which in 2022 paid $275m.

Meta is also now facing penalties that could exceed hundreds of billions of dollars stemming from COPPA violations alleged by attorneys general of 29 US states. A jury trial in the lawsuit started this week , with the Instagram and Facebook owner accused of targeting child users and profiting from them.

While the TikTok lawsuit predates last year's split of TikTok's US business and operations from its original base of China, the settlement only involves TikTok's operations in China.

ByteDance, which is a privately held company, was most recently valued by investors at $550bn .

Under the terms of the deal, TikTok and ByteDance will immediately pay the DOJ $300m. It will pay another $100m when the government vacates a 2019 consent decree with the Federal Trade Commission.

As part of the agreement, the predecessor to ByteDance, Musical.ly, was required to pay a $5.7m fine for COPPA violations and ensure it sought parental consent for any user aged under 13.

The justice department did not detail on Friday any action against TikTok beyond the fine. But the department noted that since it sued the platform, TikTok has "undergone significant changes," including to its ownership, privacy practices and platform controls for young users.

When the lawsuit was filed, attorneys for the US said there were more than 170 million teenagers using TikTok and that the app was "directed to children." Yet, it did not effectively gauge the age of users or get parental consent for use from those underage.

In 2024, former President Biden pushed for TikTok to be either banned, or have the company divest its US operations. President Donald Trump went on to support divestment of the app, which occurred last year.

Its US operations are now 81% owned by a consortium of investors, while Bytedance maintains a 19% stake.

A representative of TikTok did not respond to the BBC for comment.

articles.title: Network Rail sues companies for £5m over Llanegennech derailment
articles.summary: More than 400,000 litres of fuel spilled in the area causing an "environmental disaster".
articles.body:
Network Rail is suing two rail companies for more than £5m after a fuel spill caused by a train derailment threatened an "environmental disaster" at a designated site for protection.

The body filed a legal claim earlier this month against DB Cargo UK and Touax Rail over the derailment near Llangennech, Carmarthenshire, in August 2020.

The incident saw 10 wagons of the 25-wagon train derail , causing 446,000 litres of fuel to spill, and about 300 people had to leave the area due to the blaze.

In High Court documents, Network Rail claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" and is seeking damages for negligence.

No one was injured, but 116,000 litres of fuel ignited while 330,000 litres drained into surrounding wetlands, which form part of a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and a Special Area of Conservation.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) concluded in January 2022 that the derailment was caused by a set of wheels on one of the wagons locking, likely the result of a brake defect after "inadequate maintenance practices" were found in the investigation.

Network Rail, which owns, operates, maintains and develops Britain's railways, claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" by Touax.

It is also seeking damages from DB Cargo UK, claiming that the latter "breached a contractual duty to ensure that reasonable care was taken" in maintaining the wagon.

Lawyers for the body said it expected to recover "more than £5m" with DB Cargo and Touax yet to file defences.

A hearing in the case is due to take place.

The locomotive was pulling the wagons from Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire, to Theale, near Reading, when the derailment occurred.

The line was closed for six months after the incident and did not fully reopen for almost a year, with 30,000 tonnes of fuel-soaked soil having to be excavated.

Bill Kelly, the then-Network Rail Wales route director, said when the line fully reopened in March 2021 that work following the incident was "one of the biggest environmental recovery operations Network Rail has ever been involved with".

He added that the derailment could have caused a "total environmental disaster".

The RAIB said, in its 2022 report, that the train was travelling at about 38mph at the time of the derailment, and was carrying up to 75.5 tonnes of fuel.

The RAIB did not establish blame or liability for the incident, but made nine recommendations to avoid similar accidents.

Network Rail and DB Cargo declined to comment, while Touax has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Blood Moon partial lunar eclipse: How and when to see it in UK skies
articles.summary: There will be a partial lunar eclipse in the UK on 28 August, and may cause the Moon appear reddish in colour.
articles.body:
Skywatchers across the UK could have the chance to see a stunning partial lunar eclipse later this week as the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up in the night sky.

Lunar eclipses occur when the Moon is full which will take place in the early hours of 28 August. It may cause the full Moon - nicknamed the Sturgeon Moon - to take on an eerie reddish glow.

It comes just weeks after the UK experienced its most dramatic partial solar eclipse in nearly 30 years.

Adding to the spectacle, its position in the sky will be low on the horizon, causing a phenomenon known as the Moon illusion. This makes the Moon appear bigger and more dramatic than usual.

How and when can I see the partial lunar eclipse in the UK?

The eclipse will take place in the early hours of Friday 28 August.

The partial eclipse will begin at 03:33 BST in London, when the Moon enters Earth's darkest shadow.

It will reach its maximum at 05:12 BST, when around 90% of the Moon will be within the umbra.

By this point the Moon will be very low in the south-western sky, causing something known as the Moon illusion .

This is a term for when the Moon appears much larger than it is based on its position in the sky - an effect caused by the way our brains process visual information.

The effect is particularly noticeable during a moonrise or moonset, when the lunar disc is seen alongside familiar objects on the ground.

Exact moonset times will vary across the UK.

In London, it will set and move out of sight at approximately 06:15 BST.

A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, causing the Moon to temporarily move into the Earth's shadow.

During a partial eclipse, only part of the Moon enters the darkest section of that shadow, known as the umbra.

The Moon is not completely cut off from sunlight, however.

Sunlight passing through the Earth's atmosphere is scattered, with shorter blue wavelengths scattering more easily, while more of the longer wavelength red light reach the Moon.

These wavelengths are then reflected back towards Earth, giving the eclipsed Moon its reddish colour.

What is the weather forecast for the Blood Moon lunar eclipse?

For the best chance of seeing the eclipse, astronomers recommend finding a high location with an unobstructed view towards the south-western horizon.

Clear skies will, of course, be essential.

Viewing conditions are expected to vary considerably across the UK during the early hours of Friday morning.

With low pressure in charge, cloud and heavy showers are likely to affect some parts of the country, while other areas remain clear.

Currently, the best viewing conditions are expected across central and eastern parts of England and Wales. However, even here, the cloud cover could change a lot from one hour to the next and is very hard to forecast accurately.

You can check the latest hour-by-hour forecast where you are online or via the BBC Weather app.

articles.title: DUP MP Gregory Campbell to face expenses probe
articles.summary: The watchdog's investigation concerns the MP’s spending against their Office Costs budget.
articles.body:
The parliamentary watchdog has launched an investigation into the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Gregory Campbell over potential spending breaches.

The Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority (IPSA) said it will determine whether Campbell has been "paid an amount under the Scheme of MPs Staffing and Business Costs that should not have been allowed".

No further information will be published until the investigation has concluded.

A DUP spokesperson said: "Gregory Campbell has spent twenty-five years working for the people of East Londonderry.

"He is one of the most active constituency MPs and consistently has one of the lowest costs of NI MPs."

The party claim this is a "politicised complaint" made against Campbell about information cards and leaflets he personally distributes throughout his constituency weekly.

"Mr Campbell had already provided information about this matter and will fully cooperate with the investigation."

They added that while the process is ongoing, he "will make no further comment".

articles.title: Row breaks out over minister Anna Turley's A66 crash tribute
articles.summary: Home Office Minister Anna Turley paid tribute to all seven victims initially, sparking a backlash from the shadow justice secretary.
articles.body:
A row has broken out after a Home Office minister paid tribute to all seven victims of the deadly A66 crash.

Anna Turley, who is also MP for the area where the crash took place, was accused by shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy of placing five men who were in a car travelling on the wrong side of the road "on a par" with two police officers in an oncoming car they collided with.

All seven died in the crash near Middlesbrough in the early hours of Saturday, which detectives said resulted from "serious criminal activity".

Turley said Cleveland Police "had specifically requested" she pay tribute to all victims in any message. The force declined to confirm or deny this when contacted by the BBC.

In a letter, Turley accused Timothy of having "sought to create media hits and political points" which was "beneath contempt".

She said there was no "moral equivalence, or judgements about worth" in her tribute.

The row centres on a lengthy Facebook post Turley made shortly after the incident, in which she wrote: "This morning I went down to South Bank to lay flowers and pay my respects, on behalf of our whole community, to the seven people whose lives were so tragically cut short yesterday."

Timothy took issue with that in an X post on Monday night, saying he did not wish to "speak ill of the dead" but that "we should be able to see the difference between right and wrong".

He said it did not feel right for a Home Office minister to equate the two police officers with the men in the other car.

In her reply, Turley said she was "utterly appalled" by the accusation and said she did not know the identities of who had died at the time of her tribute, other than PCs Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38, who she named.

While she said Cleveland Police had asked her to pay tribute to all victims, the force has not confirmed this and the area's police and crime commissioner told the BBC it does not issue media advice regarding police incidents.

Police later confirmed that Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy were all in the car on the wrong side of the A66. All bar Cahill had previous convictions.

The Volkswagen Passat was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash , according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

Cleveland Police announced five more arrests on Tuesday, bringing the total to 17, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

Separately, two men previously arrested have since been charged as part of the investigation.

articles.title: UK weather: Met Office warnings in force amid thunderstorm and flood risk
articles.summary: Yellow warnings updated as torrential downpours affect parts of England and Wales, delivering some of the wettest weather in several weeks.
articles.body:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid until 22:00 BST, and was amended on Wednesday morning to cover northern and eastern Wales, as well as north-west England, the Midlands and parts of eastern and southern England.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

Another Met Office yellow warning is in place for Thursday, when more thunderstorms are expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

The Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning covers a large swathe of England and Wales.

After some early cloud and rain, sunny spells will develop across the area.

However, scattered thundery downpours will spring up during the afternoon.

As much as 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) of rain could fall in some locations within just an hour, and it is even possible that 40-50mm (1.6-2in) could accumulate over a few hours.

However, due to the hit-and-miss nature of showers, some places will miss the rain and weather apps may struggle to get the detail of the forecast correct.

Where the rain does fall, flash flooding is a real concern. This will be especially problematic where the ground is hard after the prolonged dry spell, making it difficult for the water to soak in.

Difficult driving conditions are expected with the chance that some roads could be closed.

Large hail and frequent lightning are also possible.

Northern Ireland will also see some showers but these are likely to be less intense with less thunder.

Many parts of Scotland will remain dry with sunny spells, although some showers are likely in the south-west later.

Thursday will bring another zone of thunderstorms, again affecting mostly England and Wales.

The Met Office has issued a further yellow weather warning, valid from 06:00 until 22:00 BST.

Widespread rainfall totals of 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) are expected in the warning area within three hours, while some areas could see 50mm (2in) within the same timeframe.

There is a small chance that eastern-facing hills - exposed to easterly winds - could record 75mm (3in) during 12 hours, which would bring a significant flood risk.

Gusty winds may also accompany the storms, especially in southern England on Thursday morning.

The showers may eventually reach southern Scotland and Northern Ireland but are likely to weaken and become less intense as they drift northwards.

Wettest weather in weeks for parts of southern UK

Despite a period of unsettled weather last week, some southern parts of the UK have still seen barely any rain recently.

Brize Norton in Oxfordshire has recorded just 0.4mm of rain so far this August, less than 1% of what it would normally expect during the month as a whole.

Kew Gardens recorded no rain at all in July, and only 1.8mm so far this month.

It means the rain we are expecting this week is likely to far outstrip what has fallen recently in some areas.

What does 80 per cent chance of rain mean?

Why you may not see showers and thunderstorms on your weather app

Thunderstorms are often very hit-and-miss.

Some places can see flooding downpours while others, perhaps only a few miles away, avoid the heaviest rain and stay essentially dry.

Weather apps - including the BBC Weather app - can struggle in these scenarios.

Forecasters know that the conditions are ripe for storms to form, with warm humid air across the UK interacting with a zone of colder air pushing in from the west, higher in the atmosphere.

This generates low pressure and instability.

However, the computer weather models that drive weather apps will always struggle to pinpoint exactly where and when the biggest storms will spring up.

It is a bit like heating popcorn kernels in a pan.

You cannot know precisely which kernels will pop and in which order, while some kernels may not pop at all.

Some of the storms will also occur at night, which may mean they do not show up in the daily weather icons.

It is worth keeping an eye on the hourly weather symbols, as well as the percentage chances of rain, if you are making outdoor plans.

articles.title: Empresária morre em colisão entre carro e caminhão no Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: A irmã da vítima e o motorista do caminhão foram socorridos. Acidente ocorreu na cidade de Morada Nova, no interior do estado, na manhã desta quarta-feira (26).
articles.summary: A irmã da vítima e o motorista do caminhão foram socorridos.
articles.body:
Uma colisão entre um carro e um caminhão deixou uma empresária morta e outras duas pessoas feridas na CE-138 , em Morada Nova , no interior do Ceará, na manhã desta quarta-feira (26).

Com o impacto, a condutora do carro, identificada como Vitória Guedes , ficou presa às ferragens e morreu no local. Além de empreendedora, a jovem era estudante do curso de medicina .

A irmã de Vitória, identificada como Laura Guedes, estava no banco do passageiro. Ela foi socorrida por uma equipe do Samu Ceará e levada a um hospital da região. O estado de saúde dela não foi informado.

O motorista do caminhão, que não teve a identidade informada, teve escoriações pelo corpo e foi socorrido pelo Samu sem gravidade.

Empresária e estudante de medicina, Vitória Guedes, morreu após bater o carro em um caminhão na CE-138, em Morada Nova, no interior do Ceará — Foto: Reprodução

Vitória e Laura Guedes são moradores da cidade de Jaguaribe e proprietárias da loja de roupas Alala, que possui unidades no município de origem das vítimas e na cidade de Iguatu.

A Prefeitura de Jaguaribe divulgou uma nota de pesar lamentando a morte da empresária.

"Neste momento de dor e tristeza, expressamos nossa solidariedade aos familiares e amigos, desejando força e conforto para enfrentar essa irreparável perda", disse a nota de pesar da Prefeitura de Jaguaribe.

Amigos de Vitória também prestaram homenagens a ela nas redes sociais. Em uma das publicações, uma amiga dela relatou que a empresária estava no melhor momento da vida.

"Vitória sempre foi referência de ser humano e de tudo o que ela se propunha a fazer, e ela sabia disso. Estava realizando o sonho tão aguardado de ser médica, se casou com o amor da vida dela, com lojas de sucesso e tudo o que ela sempre sonhou. De repente, tudo de desfaz de uma forma tão rápida e cruel", escreveu a amiga de Vitória.

articles.title: Alimentação inteligente melhora o desempenho e ajuda a manter a saúde  | G1
articles.standfirst: Com escolhas equilibradas e hábitos consistentes, é possível ganhar disposição e melhorar a recuperação. Covabra incentiva uma rotina mais saudável por meio do esporte
articles.summary: Com escolhas equilibradas e hábitos consistentes, é possível ganhar disposição e melhorar a recuperação. Covabra incentiva uma rotina mais saudável por meio do esporte
articles.body:
Alimentação inteligente melhora o desempenho e ajuda a manter a saúde em dia — Foto: Crédito: Divulgação Covabra

Quem pratica atividade física sabe que os resultados não dependem apenas do treino. O que vai ao prato antes e depois dos exercícios faz diferença na disposição, no rendimento e na recuperação do organismo. A boa notícia é que não é preciso seguir dietas radicais para alcançar esses benefícios: uma alimentação equilibrada e adaptada à rotina já pode trazer ganhos importantes para a saúde.

Promover esse equilíbrio faz parte do compromisso do Covabra Supermercados com o bem-estar. Além de oferecer um amplo mix de produtos para quem busca uma alimentação saudável, a rede apoia iniciativas que incentivam a prática esportiva, como a Corrida Integração, realiza o Circuito Bem-Estar Covabra nas cidades onde está presente e promove a Corrida Pequenos Incríveis Covabra, voltada às crianças.

"Nosso compromisso vai além de oferecer produtos de qualidade. Queremos incentivar escolhas que contribuam para mais saúde e qualidade de vida. Alimentação equilibrada e atividade física caminham juntas e fazem parte desse propósito", afirma Jacqueline Tavares, gerente de marketing do Covabra.

Segundo a nutricionista Juliana Porto, do Covabra, a chamada alimentação inteligente tem como principal objetivo fornecer ao organismo a energia e os nutrientes necessários para acompanhar a prática de exercícios e favorecer a recuperação. Isso significa respeitar as necessidades de cada pessoa, priorizando alimentos variados e refeições regulares, sem restrições desnecessárias.

Na prática, alguns cuidados fazem diferença. Os carboidratos continuam sendo a principal fonte de energia para o organismo durante a atividade física, enquanto as proteínas são importantes para a recuperação e a manutenção da massa muscular. Antes do treino, vale apostar em alimentos ricos em carboidratos e de fácil digestão, acompanhados de uma quantidade moderada de proteínas. Depois do exercício, o ideal é combinar carboidratos, para repor a energia, com proteínas, que auxiliam na recuperação e manutenção da massa muscular. A hidratação também merece atenção e, na maioria das situações, a água é suficiente para manter o bom funcionamento do organismo.

A especialista alerta que alguns hábitos bastante comuns podem atrapalhar os resultados, como cortar totalmente os carboidratos, exagerar no consumo de suplementos, treinar em jejum sem orientação profissional ou seguir dietas encontradas na internet. "Na maioria dos casos, uma alimentação equilibrada é suficiente para atender às necessidades nutricionais. Os suplementos devem ser utilizados apenas quando houver indicação individualizada", explica.

As boas escolhas podem começar no supermercado. Frutas, legumes, verduras, arroz, feijão, ovos, carnes magras, peixes, aveia, castanhas e laticínios naturais são alimentos que ajudam a compor uma rotina equilibrada. Para quem tem pouco tempo, combinações simples, como banana com aveia, iogurte com frutas ou um sanduíche integral com frango desfiado, também são opções práticas e nutritivas.

Mais do que buscar resultados rápidos, a alimentação inteligente está ligada à construção de hábitos que podem ser mantidos ao longo do tempo. Quando aliada à prática regular de atividades físicas, ao sono de qualidade e ao acompanhamento profissional sempre que necessário, ela contribui para uma vida mais saudável, ativa e equilibrada.

Com 36 anos de história, a rede de Supermercados Covabra (Comercial Varejista Brasileira Ltda.) foi fundada em Limeira, interior de São Paulo, em 1989. Destacou-se por implantar um novo conceito de supermercado na região e por ser pioneira no uso de tecnologia com leitores ópticos em todos os seus caixas, promovendo mais eficiência e economia para os consumidores.

Desde então, a marca não parou de investir e evoluir. Em 2017, inaugurou seu primeiro Centro de Distribuição em Sumaré (SP), com 13 mil m² de área construída, otimizando a logística e garantindo um abastecimento ainda mais eficiente para suas lojas.

Comprometida com a segurança alimentar e a sustentabilidade, a rede Covabra também passou a adotar práticas alinhadas ao RAMA (Programa de Rastreabilidade e Monitoramento de Alimentos), criado pela ABRAS (Associação Brasileira de Supermercados). O programa garante a rastreabilidade dos alimentos, monitorando aspectos como resíduos de agrotóxicos e fornecendo informações que auxiliam na seleção consciente de produtores e fornecedores.

Atualmente a rede Covabra conta com 25 lojas em 14 cidades do interior paulista (Campinas, Capivari, Indaiatuba, Itatiba, Itupeva, Jundiaí, Leme, Limeira, Pedreira, Pirassununga, Rio Claro, Valinhos, Vinhedo e Paulínia), empregando aproximadamente 5 mil funcionários e oferecendo aos clientes uma ampla variedade de produtos, com foco na qualidade, segurança e economia.

articles.title: Em vídeo de depoimento, Lito faz relato sobre a doença e família diz que tenta uso compassivo de medicamentos em teste | G1
articles.standfirst: Em vídeo divulgado hoje, ele relembra o diagnóstico e diz que família agora busca acesso a medicamentos por uso compassivo.
articles.summary: Em vídeo divulgado hoje, ele relembra o diagnóstico e diz que família agora busca acesso a medicamentos por uso compassivo.
articles.body:
Lito faz relato sobre diagnóstico e família diz que vai tentar uso compassivo de medicações em teste — Foto: Reprodução

Em vídeo divulgado nesta quarta-feira (26), Lito aparece pela primeira vez fazendo um relato pessoal sobre a doença: fala sobre o momento do diagnóstico e como tem vivido desde então, dizendo que a situação só se encerra quando a doença chegar ao fim. Ele já buscou vaga em tratamentos experimentais, mas agora a família concentra esforços em conseguir acesso aos medicamentos por uso compassivo.

"O jogo só acaba quando termina. Já vi Palmeiras virar para cima do Botafogo muito depois do tempo regulamentar e vocês sabem que eu sou um homem de ciência, mas também sou um homem de muita fé. E a gente não sabe o que pode acontecer", disse em vídeo.

Lito foi diagnosticado com a doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob, doença é rara, não tem cura, evolui rapidamente e compromete ao mesmo tempo a cognição e os movimentos do paciente. Diferente da maior parte dos pacientes, ele perdeu primeiro os movimentos, mas mantém a cognição. No vídeo, ele aparece em cadeira de rodas, com dificuldade motora nas mãos.

Ele diz que não tem medo de morrer, mas que busca por algo porque não sabe como dizer ao filho que "vai virar estrelinha".

Antes de buscar o uso compassivo, a família de Lito tentou uma vaga nos próprios estudos. Os tratamentos experimentais agem sobre esse processo usando uma estratégia central: reduzir a quantidade da proteína normal que serve de matéria-prima para essa desordem que intoxica o cérebro.

O ION717, da farmacêutica americana Ionis Pharmaceuticals.

E o PRiSM, conduzido pelo Broad Institute, ligado a Harvard e ao MIT.

Os dois miram o mesmo alvo — reduzir a produção da proteína príon que se acumula no cérebro —, mas usam tecnologias diferentes para tentar chegar lá.

As respostas, porém, não abriram caminho. A Ionis Pharmaceuticals informou que não há vagas abertas para novos voluntários no ION717 e que a empresa não autoriza o uso compassivo da substância — possibilidade que a família chegou a cogitar.

Já os responsáveis pelo PRiSM sinalizaram que ele poderia integrar o estudo, mas como parte do grupo controle, sem receber o medicamento.

Nesta quarta-feira (26), em vídeo, a esposa de Lito, Mila Seidl, disse que eles vão continuar tentando o uso compassivo das medicações após as negativas.

O uso compassivo é o mecanismo que permite a um paciente ter acesso a um medicamento que ainda está em fase de testes, mesmo sem fazer parte oficialmente do estudo clínico. Na prática, é uma exceção: a pessoa recebe uma substância ainda não aprovada porque não há, no momento, alternativa terapêutica capaz de deter a doença.

No caso de Lito, a doença não tem nenhum tratamento conhecido e aprovado.

Porém, essa concessão não é automática. Ela depende de uma série de etapas, como a avaliação da saúde do paciente, o aval médico da farmacêutica responsável pelo medicamento e a autorização das agências sanitárias envolvidas.

A Ionis, farmacêutica que o estudo está mais avançado já negou a possibilidade de uso compassivo. Ainda assim, a família disse que tentaria esse caminho.

articles.title: O que atrai turistas à região atingida por avalanche no Nepal? | G1
articles.standfirst: Rasuwa abriga uma das rotas de acesso ao Monte Kailash, considerado sagrado pelos hindus, e também parte de Langtang, região conhecida por trilhas, geleiras e lagos de altitude.
articles.summary: Rasuwa abriga uma das rotas de acesso ao Monte Kailash, considerado sagrado pelos hindus, e também parte de Langtang, região conhecida por trilhas, geleiras e lagos de altitude.
articles.body:
A inundação repentina que atingiu o Nepal e o Tibete nesta quarta-feira (26) deixou cerca de 403 desaparecidos no Nepal, sendo 341 deles estrangeiros, segundo o Conselho de Turismo do país.

Um dos distritos mais atingidos foi Rasuwa, no norte do Nepal, próximo à fronteira com o Tibete. Além dos desaparecidos, a inundação deixou 95 mortos e atingiu vilarejos e áreas turísticas da região.

A presença de tantos turistas na região pode ser explicada por dois principais fatores:

Região atinmgida por avalanche no nepal atrai turistas — Foto: Reprodução/GloboNews

Situado a 6.718 metros acima do nível do mar, o monte Kailash, no Tibete, é um local sagrado para hindus, budistas e jainista — Foto: Wikimedia Commons

O Monte Kailash, que fica no Tibete, é considerado sagrado pelo hinduísmo e outras religiões . Todos os anos, milhares de peregrinos viajam até a região para visitar a montanha.

Uma das formas de chegar ao local é pelo Nepal. Os viajantes seguem até Rasuwa e cruzam a fronteira entre Nepal e China pelo posto de Rasuwagadhi. Do outro lado da fronteira fica a região de Gyirong de onde a viagem continua em direção ao Monte Kailash.

Segundo a Associated Press, muitos dos turistas desaparecidos após a inundação desta quarta-feira eram peregrinos que seguiam para o Monte Kailash, principalmente vindos da Índia. Segundo o Conselho de Turismo do Nepal, ao menos 105 dos desaparecidos são indianos.

Ao New York Times, um iogue indiano conhecido como Sadhguru afirmou que 77 integrantes de grupos organizados por sua fundação estavam no centro de imigração da fronteira entre Nepal e Tibete quando a inundação atingiu o local. Até o momento, ele ainda não conseguiu contato com o grupo.

Rasuwa também atrai visitantes por abrigar parte da região de Langtang, uma das áreas de trekking do Himalaia nepalês. Localizada a cerca de 130 quilômetros ao norte de Katmandu, próxima à fronteira com o Tibete, a região reúne montanhas de grande altitude, vales, geleiras e lagos.

Entre os destaques está o Langtang Lirung, de 7.245 metros, o pico mais alto da área. Segundo o Conselho de Turismo do Nepal, Langtang possui ainda mais de 70 geleiras de diferentes tamanhos e lagos de altitude, como Gosainkunda, Parvatikunda, Bhairavkunda e Dudhkunda.

Langtang Lirung no Nepal — Foto: Wikimedia Commons

As trilhas pela região também passam por florestas de vegetação temperada e subalpina e por vilarejos onde vivem comunidades tamang, grupo étnico tradicional da região. Além das paisagens, o turismo em Langtang é associado ao contato com a cultura local, incluindo idioma, vestimentas, arquitetura e artesanato.

Por ficar relativamente perto de Katmandu, Langtang é apontada pelo Conselho de Turismo do Nepal como um dos destinos de trekking mais acessíveis a partir da capital. A região, porém, recebe menos visitantes do que algumas das rotas de trekking mais famosas do país, o que também é citado pelo órgão como uma característica do destino.

Lago Gosainkunda no Nepal — Foto: Wikimedia Commons

articles.title: Teenager, 15, arrested over fatal stabbing at Brent Civic Centre
articles.summary: The victim, believed to be a 17-year-old, was found fatally injured at Brent Council's headquarters.
articles.body:
A 15-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a young man was found fatally stabbed in a building which houses Brent Council's headquarters and a library.

Emergency services were called at about 14:30 BST on Tuesday to Brent Civic Centre, near Wembley Stadium in north-west London, where the victim was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said he had not yet been formally identified but he is believed to be 17-year-old David Wynter.

The boy was arrested on Tuesday, 25 August and is being held in police custody.

On Wednesday, one man who works in the area told BBC London the stabbing "felt normal".

"These things happen every single day here, in London and in the area. It's not a big surprise," he said.

"You see things like this happen all the time. You read the news and every single day there's something going on. If it's in Harrow, or Wembley, or Neasden, or Willesden or wherever, it doesn't come as a surprise."

However, one woman who lives in the area said the stabbing "came as a shock".

"I've never felt unsafe around here and it's a bit concerning," she said.

Student Demi said he felt "uneasy" after the stabbing.

"It's not really an unsafe area," he said. "It's a bit out of the ordinary.

"These things happen, unfortunately, but it's a bit strange to have it happen here."

Kate, another local resident, said: "Usually we feel very safe. We're fortunate living in this area because there are lots of security patrols and there are always people around.

"Stabbings are terrible tragedies, but it could happen anywhere, and I know there are areas of London that have to deal with that every day.

"I still feel safe. We're fortunate to live here with so much security; I wish that everyone lived in such an area."

Muhammed Butt, leader of Brent Council, said on Tuesday that the borough had been "shaken" by the "appalling and deeply tragic incident".

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim, their family and loved ones, as well as the staff, residents and visitors who witnessed what happened," he said.

Butt said the Civic Centre would remain closed until further notice.

A Section 60 order is now in force across eight Brent wards, giving police enhanced stop and search powers.

It runs from 15:00 BST on Wednesday until 03:30 BST on Thursday.

Supt Chris Clarke, the Met's lead for emergency response policing in the area, said the force was urgently working to identify the victim and inform his next of kin.

"We recognise the concern this incident will cause within the local community and are committed to keeping residents informed as our inquiries progress," he said.

"In light of the incident, we have authorised additional stop-and-search powers to help prevent further violence, support our investigation, and keep people safe.

"There will be an increased police presence in and around the area in the coming hours while our officers continue their investigation."

articles.title: V&A museum workers to strike in September over pay and conditions
articles.summary: Workers at three Victoria and Albert museum sites are due to strike and further staff plan to work to rule.
articles.body:
Workers at three Victoria and Albert museum sites in London will strike next month over pay, health and safety, and working conditions.

Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union members at V&A East Storehouse, V&A East and Young V&A are due to walk out on 4 and 5 September.

From 4 September onwards, PCS members at all sites will work to rule and withdraw cooperation in coordinated action with Prospect, another trade union, PCS said.

A V&A spokesperson said the museum had been negotiating with the unions since February and had met the majority of their demands with "a significantly improved offer".

A PCS ballot registered 95% in favour of industrial action. The union did not say how many workers would be striking.

It called for better pay, a cross-site policy to close public spaces when temperatures reached 30C, and for V&A East Storehouse workers "to drink and carry water at work".

Fran Heathcote, PCS general secretary, said members had given the V&A "every opportunity" to resolve the dispute through negotiation and if management wanted to avoid further disruption, it needed to get around the table with PCS "and start negotiating seriously".

The V&A spokesperson said they valued their staff enormously and were committed to providing safe and supportive work environments.

"Our latest pay offer delivers a pay rise well above inflation for all staff, with an average 4.2% pay rise and a 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues."

They said the V&A had a longstanding commitment to paying at least the London Living Wage.

"All our staff have regular breaks, and access to drinking fountains on each floor is provided at V&A East Storehouse, which has an air-cooling system.

"Extensive heatwave mitigation has also been put in place across our museums."

Visitors are advised to check museum websites for updates on any disruption.

articles.title: Guernsey Dolly Parton superfan's grief for his 'fairy godmother'
articles.summary: Lee Smith, who has an extensive memorabilia collection, says the news has left him "devastated".
articles.body:
A man whose home is packed with Dolly Parton memorabilia said he was "devastated" by the death of the country music icon.

Lee Smith, 36, from Guernsey, has spent nearly two decades building his Dolly Parton collection featuring signed albums, dolls, perfume, wigs, records and replicas inspired by the singer.

Speaking among shelves filled with memorabilia, Smith said: "I was devastated. I didn't believe it at first."

He said Parton's storytelling and songwriting had inspired him and helped give him confidence as a teenager. He said she had felt "almost like a fairy godmother".

Parton, whose career spanned more than 60 years, died aged 80 following a brief battle with cancer.

She wrote more than 3,000 songs and sold more than 100 million records worldwide. She was also known for her charitable work, including her Imagination Library literacy programme.

Now, alongside fans paying tribute around the world, Smith said he was mourning a star who had been part of his life for nearly 20 years.

Smith, who has a leg tattoo in honour of Parton, said his admiration for the singer began when he was seven years old, listening to her music on cassette tapes in the car with his parents.

Smith said the music remained the most important part of her legacy.

"My favourite piece of my collection? I'm going to say it is just the music," he said.

Smith met Parton once at Wembley Arena in London when he was 17.

"It was only five minutes, but that five minutes felt like a whole hour," he said.

articles.title: Tourist board says 33 UK nationals missing after Nepal-Tibet flash floods
articles.summary: Flooding and mud slides hit the Rasuaw region in the morning on Wednesday, killing at least 95 people, Nepali police said.
articles.body:
Thirty-three people from the UK are among hundreds feared missing following a deadly flash flood near the Nepal-Tibet border.

Flooding and mud slides hit the Rasuaw region in the morning on Wednesday, killing at least 95 people in Nepal and three in Tibet, according to Chinese state media.

Nepal police said 579 tourists are missing - including 466 who are foreign nationals, from 28 different countries.

The UK Foreign Office said it is working closely with Nepalese authorities "following concerning reports of British nationals who are missing" and has encouraged Brits to follow local guidance and "remain alert to the changing situation".

According to Nepal police, 113 of the missing tourists are Nepalese, and 54 are from the US.

Excursion company Alpine Eco Trek, which offers guided expeditions and tours in Nepal, told the Press Association (PA) that 12 British nationals on its tour in the region - as well as two Irish nationals - were on an excursion across the Nepal-Tibet border and are believed to be missing.

Manager Kumar Adhikari said there was "not much info to share at the moment, but yes we have 12 British citizens (supposed) to make entry this morning".

According to the company's travel logs, shared with PA, the age of the missing British citizens ranges from 13 to 65.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he is "deeply concerned" by news of the flash flooding, and wrote on social media: "All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home".

In a joint statement with Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland, the UK embassy in Nepal urged British nationals in Nepal to "exercise caution in affected areas".

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu, with preliminary information suggesting it was caused by an earthquake triggering an avalanche with melted snow pouring into the Bhote Koshi river.

Dramatic CCTV footage showed a wall of water and mud hitting buildings near a border crossing and video filmed from inside a bus in Trishuli captured dozens of people trying to flee a flood surge that was surging through the valley.

Meanwhile Chinese state media outlet CCTV said a mudslide in Tibet's Gyirong killed three people and left 265 missing, with rescue efforts under way.

articles.title: WATCH: The Terrifying Moment A Wall Of Water Swallows An Entire Village On The Nepal China Border
articles.summary: A massive rush of water and debris hit villages in mountainous regions of Nepal near the country’s border with China, claiming 31 lives and leaving hundreds...
articles.body:
A massive rush of water and debris hit villages in mountainous regions of Nepal near the country's border with China, claiming 31 lives and leaving hundreds missing, including some tourists, officials say.

A video uploaded to Nepal Police's official account and verified by media outlets shows people running away from a rush of water that destroys a whole valley in less than a second. The footage shows houses, roads, bridges, and construction projects being swept away by rushing water.

The flash flooding originated on the Tibetan side of the Bhote Koshi River, entered Nepal around 9 a.m. local time, and first hit Rasuwa District, followed by the neighboring districts of Nuwakot and Dhading.

According to officials, an earthquake might have triggered a massive rock and ice avalanche that blocked the flow and created a dangerous surge of water going downstream. Officials warn that the cause is still under investigation, and debris that blocks the way could trigger another flood.

Helicopters used for rescue missions could not land in the areas hit by the flood because the river level is much higher than usual, and rescue teams cannot reach towns that became unreachable because of flooded roads.

384 travelers, including 291 foreigners, were registered as missing as authorities investigate their safety, according to the Nepal Tourism Board. The board says the police forces responsible for tourists and travel agencies are working to locate all visitors who were in or passed through the affected area.

The disaster affected even the neighboring state. A mudslide hit the Gyirong crossing point and caused road, communications, and electricity blackouts in the Shigatse region of Tibet, according to Xinhua News Agency. Chinese officials reported that there might be many casualties in Tibet.

Nepal Electricity Authority reports that several power plants and transmission lines are destroyed and electricity supply is interrupted in the affected districts.

Later on Wednesday, a spokesman for Nepal Police told AFP that the number of fatalities increased to 95, of whom around 30 are police personnel.

Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have been deployed for a search and rescue operation. Officials stated that more fatalities may happen as rescuers reach the villages farther downstream.

articles.title: Rupert Grint to return to Harry Potter in Broadway play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
articles.summary: Grint, now 38, will play his character as an adult in the Harry Potter spin-off play in New York.
articles.body:
Harry Potter star Rupert Grint is to return to the role of Ron Weasley - playing the character as an adult in the spin-off play in New York.

Grint was first cast to play Ron in the original films at the age of 11. Now 38, he will join the cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on Broadway for four months from next February.

The play catches up with Harry, Ron and Hermione as grown-ups, 19 years after the end of the events in the original books and films - with Ron and Hermione now married and sending their daughter to Hogwarts.

"Dusting off the old robes. New York - see you all in February," Grint wrote on Instagram .

Last November, he told BBC News he was unlikely to ever "step out" of Ron Weasley's shadow. "I'm fine with that. I think it's great," he said.

In a statement on Wednesday, the British actor said: "Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can't wait to meet him again in this stage of life.

"There is something so full-circle and so special about stepping back into Ron's shoes now when we are both fathers; it is somehow both very familiar and completely new.

"And the joy of being back on Broadway, this time in a role that defined so much of my life is truly exciting."

Grint is the only one of the main three stars from the films to return to their roles, although co-star Tom Felton is currently reprising his role as Draco Malfoy in the same play.

They are not due to appear on stage together, however - Felton will appear until 3 January, with Grint joining on 2 February. He is currently scheduled to appear until 30 May.

Grint appeared in all eight Harry Potter films between 2001 and 2011, and has since starred in TV shows including Sick Note, Snatch and Servant.

He also acted on Broadway in the comedy It's Only a Play in 2014.

Harry Potter and the Cursed Child producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender said Grint's performances in the Potter films "defined for generations what it meant to be a loyal and brave friend even in the face of adversity and hardship".

They added: "Rupert is not simply revisiting a role from his past. He is continuing a journey he began as a child and carrying it forward with all the life and experience he has gained since filming concluded, including a career that has taken him from film to television to acclaimed stage work on both Broadway and the West End."

articles.title: Mural celebrates 'legends' of Ipswich Town
articles.summary: Artist Bradley Lloyd says he wanted to celebrate the diversity of the club and its iconic moments.
articles.body:
A mural celebrating the history and diversity of Ipswich Town FC is in place close to the club's ground.

Town fan Bradley Lloyd designed the artwork, which was chosen from a shortlist by supporters and installed in Princes Street, opposite Portman Road.

The mural was unveiled ahead of Town's first match back in the Premier League at home to Sunderland on Saturday .

Lloyd said: "I really wanted to show club legends, celebrate the diversity of the town, plus show iconic moments, like Terry Butcher playing for England and Russell Osman in the Escape to Victory kit, with this in mind."

A competition welcomed proposals from artists, designers and creatives to fill an 170 sq m (1,830 sq ft) wooden hoarding and transform the site into a vibrant and proud display of civic and club identity, celebrating the spirit of Ipswich.

Lloyd said: "'Us and our people' was a quote by captain Dara O'Shea that stuck in my head at the end of last season.

"Wolsey's Gate took a lot of time to get the bricks right, but needed to be on there. It was all drawn digitally and took a few months to get to the final design.

"It looks great and I'm really happy with it."

Andrew Wood, chief revenue officer at Ipswich Town FC and Ipswich Central board member, said: "We are delighted that so many supporters are now able to see a piece of art which represents all that's good about Ipswich Town.

"It's a fantastic addition to matchdays at Portman Road and to the town in general."

articles.title: Empty Gosport theatre bought by council put up for sale
articles.summary: The former bingo hall has stood empty for several years and cost more than £1m in bills.
articles.body:
An empty theatre bought by a council four years ago has been put up for sale.

The Criterion Theatre on Forton Road, Gosport, was purchased for £600,000 in 2022 and earmarked to become a multi-purpose entertainment venue.

At the time, Liberal Democrat council leader Peter Chegwyn said no council taxpayers' money was spent on the theatre itself, although the building would need substantial investment.

Current Conservative leader of the council Zoe Huggins said she could not justify further spending while facing a £3.3m structural deficit.

Her administration proposed the sale of the building, and the decision was voted for by councillors in July. For sale signs have now gone up outside the building.

Reform UK councillor James Figgins said: "I'm really pleased to see the Criterion now up for sale.

"This is an exciting opportunity for Gosport that, with the right investment and vision, could bring a real boost to our town."

The former bingo hall has stood empty for several years and cost more than £1m in professional fees, works and ongoing bills.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , Figgins said residents had repeatedly raised the future of the building with him.

The building first opened in 1912 and was run as a cinema and theatre until 1968. It then became a bingo hall and closed in March 2020.

Chegwyn has been contacted for further comment.

articles.title: We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy
articles.summary: Stacy Hunter was killed by her estranged husband weeks after he was released on bail - her family wish the authorities had intervened further.
articles.body:
Stacy Hunter's family saw clear signs that she was being manipulated, controlled and abused by her estranged husband Jim Mair long before he murdered her.

Mair "dictated" what was happening in Stacy's life, used her three children as leverage, threatened suicide, and took his violent temper out on objects in the house - without laying a hand on Stacy directly.

Her brother Sean wanted to intervene and help her, but he worried about being too "full on" and potentially causing more harm.

Her mother Ann wanted to be around to support her daughter and look after her grandchildren, but worried Mair would see her as trying to "interfere".

"He can take that away from you and make it harder to be in touch," Ann said.

Stacy's family said that when the 35-year-old attempted to leave the marriage, Mair became more violent.

Last month, Mair murdered Stacy at her home near Houston. His body was found next to hers.

Three weeks before this, he had appeared in court accused of strangling her and was released on bail.
